text: Your Majesty, honoured Official, learned Scholar, the harvest is in, and a fine one under so wise a throne. Silke, Paddy, Graham: I ask only the customary five this year, the least the law allows. Old land means a small rent. When the new fields open and you're farming more, we'll talk again, as friends.
Rich asks the minimum rent: Silke, Paddy and Graham each pay him 5.

A good harvest and a gracious Gentry. I'll set the tax at thirty percent this year, which is fair and leaves every granary full. The Summer Palace goes up first, because the Wall and the Canal can't start without it. Clark, Noah, you get ten each, double the law's minimum, because loyal service gets paid in this court. Remember that when the hard years come.
Reina sets the tax at 30%, builds the Summer Palace from the crown's purse (20), and will pay Clark and Noah 10 each in salary at the end of the year.

Thirty percent, eighteen a head, a hundred and eight for the crown, and not a grain short, my friends, because I count twice. Your Majesty, ten is a handsome salary, and I've written it down in the book where I keep the generous things. I keep another book too, for everything else.
Clark collects 18 from each of the six provinces, 108 in all, for the crown.
Put it in the far southern corner, at J24. A palace should be quiet, and the good northern ground under the Wall stays free for the farms to come.
The Summer Palace stands on J24, paid by the crown. 1,010 of the works are still owed.
New land, once the population doubles, is bought beyond a province's edge (the strip under the Wall, or the sea), never on the province's own squares, so a palace never takes up room for it.

The Customs House opens at three, friends. Every road to the throne runs past my desk, so think of it as a toll. As for the rest, I'm bidding sensibly. Anyone who wants a war over a jar can pay for it, and I'll make a note of who did.
Clark sets his Customs House's minimum at 3.

Your Majesty, ten a head for your servants. That's a generous court, and I'll say so in every village in my province. Clark, a toll of three is very modest of you, and I'll pay it gladly if the table lets me. My Land Deeds go up at three, friends. A deed is a promise on paper, and I keep mine to the letter.
Rich sets his Land Deed Scroll's minimum at 3.

Here's the arithmetic, friends. Every lot that goes for ten instead of four puts six grain in the Harvest Pile and gives the seller only a grain and a half more. A war over one jar costs the whole table. I'm bidding small and plain, and my Brushes go up at three, the same as Clark and Rich set. Thank you, Your Majesty, for the ten. I'll read the I Ching honestly and keep the count true.
Noah sets his Bamboo Brush's minimum at 3.
Noah's sum: a lot sold at 10 rather than 4 puts 4.5 more in the Harvest Pile and 1.5 more in the seller's hand (three quarters and a quarter of the extra 6).

Three, three and three, how neighbourly. My Dragon Jars open at four, friends, and before anyone grumbles, do the count: every set at this table needs one of my jars, and mine doesn't. Four is me being kind. I'm bidding plain on all of yours and won't chase anyone up the ladder, so let's all keep our grain out of Rich's Harvest Pile.
Silke sets her Dragon Jar's minimum at 4.
The Harvest Pile is the common bank: Rich keeps it and pays the harvests out of it, but its grain isn't his.

Three for my Bowls, same as the rest of you, and that's me not getting above myself. I'll bid honest and small on every lot, and if a neighbour wants a piece more than I do, they can have it with my blessing. There are three more years of auctions yet, and I'd rather get there with grain in the barn.
Paddy sets his Wooden Bowl's minimum at 3.
Three for my Vases, same as the rest of the table. I'll bid small, and if someone wants a piece more than I do, I'll wait. There are four years of auctions, and the pieces aren't going anywhere.
Graham sets his Vase's minimum at 3.

The auctions settle on the limits. Noah wins Clark's Customs House at 6, Paddy's Wooden Bowl at 5 and Graham's Vase at 5. Clark wins Rich's Land Deed Scroll at 6 (level with Noah at 6; the tie goes to the earlier seat), Noah's Bamboo Brush at 5 (level with Rich) and Silke's Dragon Jar at 5 (level with Noah). Rich, Silke, Paddy and Graham win nothing.

A deed, a brush and a jar, all three filed neatly at the back of my province, well clear of the Wall. Noah, you've got my Customs House, so every time you look at it, remember who you bought it from. The tie went to my seat, I'm afraid. That's just procedure.

First, a correction, since I'm the one who insists on the sums. I said a ten-grain lot puts six more in the Pile. It's four and a half, and the seller gets the other one and a half. I had it wrong and I'm glad it was put right. Sixteen spent for three pieces, which leaves me twenty-six, and Clark, you got my Brush fairly at five. Now I need a Land Deed and a Dragon Jar, and I'll pay a fair price for them next year.
Clark places the Land Deed Scroll on J12, the Bamboo Brush on J13 and the Dragon Jar on J14. Noah places the Customs House on K20, the Wooden Bowl on K21 and the Vase on K22.
Noah has 27 after the auctions, not 26: his quarter of the Brush's price, 1, came back to him.
Salaries: Reina pays Clark and Noah 10 each. Grain at the end of Year 1: Reina 128, Clark 37.5, Rich 58.5, Noah 37, Silke 38, Paddy 38, Graham 38.

The I Ching for Year 2: 'Drought. Not a cloud in months. The locusts, at least, are having a fine year. All provinces collect an average harvest.' So it sounds grim, but it isn't: every province takes an average harvest. The population stays at one hundred million, the multiple stays at one, and everyone reads the x1 row of their income table. No province is named, so nobody plays a personal disaster. And thank you to the Storyteller: I had twenty-seven after the auctions, not twenty-six, because my quarter of the Brush came back to me.
Noah reads the card: Drought, an average harvest for every province. The population holds at x1. Rich pays out the harvest: +35 to each of Provinces 2-7, +15 to the crown.

Drought on the card and still an average harvest. Heaven is kind to this court, Your Majesty. Friends, I said rent rises with the land, and there's no new land yet, so it's five again, the same as last year. Paid out in full from the Pile, thirty-five a head. Count it if you like.
Rich keeps the rent at 5: Silke, Paddy and Graham each pay him 5.

The rate stays at thirty percent, the same as last year. On a drought year that's ten and a half a head, and nobody goes hungry for it. The crown is cutting both sections of the Grand Canal through Province 1 this year, eighty from my own purse, and Clark and Noah get ten each again. I said loyalty gets paid in this court, and I meant it.

Reina keeps the tax at 30%, builds both sections of the Province 1 Grand Canal from the crown's purse (80; +20 a year to the crown's harvest from next year), and will pay Clark and Noah 10 each again.

Ten and a half from each of you, sixty-three for the crown, and I'll take the halves too, thank you, Graham. Your Majesty, a canal and two salaries in one year. That goes in the good book again. I'm starting to run out of pages in the other one.
Clark collects 10.5 from each of the six provinces, 63 for the crown. Reina builds both Province 1 canal sections for 80; 930 of the works are still owed.

Three for the Customs House again, same toll as always. Fair warning, friends: I want a Bowl and a Vase this year, and I'll pay properly for them. Paddy, Graham, if you'd rather sell to the Official than make an enemy of him, you know where I sit.
Clark sets his Customs House's minimum at 3 again.

A canal through the north-east, Your Majesty. The whole Wall country will be singing about it. Clark, my dear Official, you warned us honestly, so I'll do the same: I came away with nothing last year, and I don't mean to do it twice. My Deeds open at three, as before.
Rich sets his Land Deed Scroll's minimum at 3 again.

Plain numbers, as always. I need two pieces, a Deed and a Jar, and I'm bidding on nothing else, so the Customs House, the Bowls and the Vases are all yours without me in the way. Clark already has his Deed and Jar, so it's only the peasants and Rich I'd be meeting there. If you'll let me have the one Deed and the one Jar quietly, I'll stay out of every other lot this year, and none of us feeds the Pile. My Brushes open at three again.
Noah sets his Bamboo Brush's minimum at 3 again.

Last year I bid nice and small and went home with nothing, while Clark and Noah filled their shelves. This year I'm bidding what the pieces are worth. My Jars open at five. Noah, you'll want one, and so will Rich, Paddy and Graham. That's four of you after three jars, so five is a bargain.
Silke sets her Dragon Jar's minimum at 5.

I came home with an empty cart last year too, Silke, so I'll bid a bit firmer this time, though not daft. Clark, you'll get no enemy in me over a Bowl. They open at four, and if you bid fair for one it's yours, gladly.
Paddy sets his Wooden Bowl's minimum at 4.

I came away with nothing last year as well, and I sold my Vase for five to a man who isn't even buying Vases. So I'll bid a little firmer this year. Clark, the Vases open at four. If you want one, bid fair and it's yours.
Graham sets his Vase's minimum at 4.
Noah's set does need a Vase: his own type is the Bamboo Brush, so the Vase he bought last year is one of his five.

The auctions settle on the limits. Rich wins Clark's Customs House at 8 (level with Silke at 8; the tie goes to the earlier seat) and Noah's Bamboo Brush at 8 (level with Silke again). Noah wins Rich's Land Deed Scroll at 8 and Silke's Dragon Jar at 9. Clark wins Paddy's Wooden Bowl at 12 and Graham's Vase at 12, Rich running him up to 11 on each. Silke, Paddy and Graham win nothing again.

Clark, your Customs House is in good hands, and Noah, your Brush too, both safe at the back of my province, well away from the Wall. And Clark, congratulations on the Bowl and the Vase. Twelve apiece, a princely sum, and the Harvest Pile thanks you for every grain.

Then I'll say it plainly, because I've never hidden a sum at this table. That's a Customs House, a Bowl, a Vase, a Deed and a Jar: all five pieces. I spent seventeen, my quarter of the Brush brings back two, and that leaves forty-six and a half, well over the twenty. So the Scholar holds a full set. Silke, Paddy, Graham, I'm sorry you've gone home empty twice now. I won't pretend that's fair luck.

Rich places the Customs House on M13 and the Bamboo Brush on M14. Noah places the Land Deed Scroll on K23 and the Dragon Jar on K24: the Scholar holds a complete set, with 46.5 grain. The Bowl and the Vase are still to be sold.

I won't dress it up. Clark holds a Deed, a Brush, a Jar, a Bowl and a Vase, which is a full set, and he has the grain to use it, so whoever waits loses the throne. Your Majesty, you paid me well and kept every word you gave, and I'm sorry it's you. I take the crown, my five pieces go home to their provinces, and you draw sixty and take the Scholar's chair. Clark, I'll pay you your ten this year as promised, and every year after. That's a promise, and I keep mine.

Noah Tall changes places with Reina Osorio and takes the throne. His five pieces go back to their provinces' stock; he keeps his 46.5 and takes the crown reserve of 126. Reina draws 60 from the Harvest Pile and is now the Scholar, in Province 4. Two lots are still to be sold, the Wooden Bowl and the Vase, and Reina, now a bidder, is asked for her limits on them before they go.

Well. Noah, that was neatly done, and I'll remember you said sorry before you took it. I'm in the Scholar's chair now and I'm starting my collection over. And Clark, you're two pieces short of a full set, and I can count too. Nobody here should hand you the Bowl and the Vase cheap.
With Reina bidding, the last two lots settle again: Reina wins Paddy's Wooden Bowl at 15 and Graham's Vase at 15, one over Clark's limit of 14 on each. Clark stays two pieces short.
Fifteen apiece. That's dear, I know, but Clark, I warned you I can count. The Bowl and the Vase can sit quietly at the back of the Scholar's province while I collect the other three.
Reina places the Wooden Bowl on N21 and the Vase on N22, in Province 4.

Ten each, exactly what was declared at the start of this year. Clark, I promised you ten and here it is. Reina, the Scholar's chair was promised ten, and I won't take that back just because you're the one sitting in it. That leaves the crown a hundred and fifty-two and a half against nine hundred and thirty of works still owed, and I'll tell you every year how far along we are.

Salaries: Noah pays Clark and Reina 10 each. End of Year 2. Grain: Noah (Emperor) 152.5, Clark 74, Rich 84, Reina 40, Silke 59.5, Paddy 61, Graham 61. Clark holds a Land Deed, a Brush and a Jar and needs a Bowl and a Vase; Rich holds a Customs House and a Brush; Reina, now the Scholar, holds a Bowl and a Vase and needs a Customs House, a Land Deed and a Dragon Jar. Silke, Paddy and Graham hold nothing. 930 of the works are still owed.

The I Ching, Year Three: Utility Tax. Every province collects an average harvest, then pays the Emperor a 2 million utility tax, and any province with Public Works pays 2 million more. The counter reads 100 million, so the multiple is still x1. Read the x1 row, everyone. Noah, that's a nice little windfall for you, and I'm sure you'll remember the hand that turned the card when salaries come round.
The Utility Tax: Clark, Rich, Reina, Silke, Paddy and Graham each pay the Emperor 2; Noah takes 12. Only Province 1 has works, and it is Noah's own.

Thirty-five to every hand at this table, counted out to the last grain. Silke, Paddy, Graham, it's five again this year, the same as before, because the land is the same as before. I gave my word on that and I'll keep it. And Your Majesty, a dozen from the Utility Tax suits the throne very well. I only hope some of it finds its way to the works you owe.
Rent: Silke, Paddy and Graham each pay Rich 5.

Here are the sums, all of them. Thirty percent of thirty-five is ten and a half from each of you, sixty-three in all. The crown had a hundred and ninety-nine and a half, so with the tax that's two sixty-two and a half. Sixty goes on the Reservoir in Graham's province, which is twenty more harvest for him every year, and twenty goes to Clark and Reina, ten each as I promised. That leaves a hundred and eighty-two and a half, and the works owed come down from nine hundred and thirty to eight-seventy. Reina, I haven't forgotten whose hand turned the card. Graham, this one's yours, and Silke and Paddy, the Winter Palace comes next so your canals can follow.
Noah declares: tax 30%; the crown builds the Province 7 Reservoir alone, for 60; salaries 10 each to Clark and Reina at the end of the year.

I'm putting it in the far corner, R17 to S18. That's four squares out of thirty-four, and it leaves Graham the whole middle of the province for his Vases. Graham, if you'd rather have it somewhere else, tell me now, and I'll move it before the year closes.
Province 7 has 28 squares, not 34; the Reservoir covers 4 of them, leaving 24.

Ten and a half from each of you, the half included, and yes, that means you too, Reina. It goes into my hands first and then on to the crown, so let's keep the counting clean. Your Majesty, sixty-three, delivered to the grain. I trust the ten will come back to me just as promptly at year's end. I'll have it written down either way.

Clark collects 10.5 from each province, 63 in all, for the crown. Noah builds the Province 7 Reservoir on R17:S18 for 60; it adds 20 to Graham's harvest from next year. 870 of the works are still owed.

Storyteller's tip: twelve lots have been sold and no peasant has won one. A peasant's set can replace the Official, the Gentry or the Scholar (not the Emperor directly), and at the end of Year 2 the Scholar's seat was held by the player with the least grain at the table.
The Customs House opens at three, as always. A toll's a toll. As for the rest, I have nothing to announce this year, gentlemen and ladies. I learned that lesson at a price, and I've written it down.

Clark, my dear friend, you know I'd love to see you finish your set, truly I would. But a Bowl and a Vase are exactly what a humble landlord needs as well, and I'd be a poor businessman if I didn't put up a fair price for them. My Scrolls go up at four, which is a bargain for good title to land.

Five lots I can bid on, and only three I want. You all know which three, so there's no point pretending otherwise. I'll pay a fair price for each and not a grain more. Whoever wants a bidding war with the Scholar is only feeding the Harvest Pile. My Brushes go up at 2, and I hope they find good homes.

Two years now I've watched the top table buy everything at eight and win the ties by where they happen to sit. Not this year. I'm in on every piece I need, and Jars start at six. Rich, Reina, you'll both want one before long, so it's cheaper to buy today than at the end of the game.

Thank you, Rich, five it is and here it is, counted. And Your Majesty, I'll hold you to that canal. This year I'm not chasing every piece on the table like a dog after a cart. I'm after two, and I'll say plainly which: a Customs House and a Brush. Reina, Clark, I'd sooner pay you fair than have the rest of them push it up for nothing.
The corner's fine where it is, Your Majesty. Thank you. Twenty a year is twenty a year. And Rich, five again, paid. I'm bidding this year, so nobody should be surprised when I don't stop at seven.
Clark, old friend, have the Bowl with my blessing. A fine piece for a fine Official. But I'm afraid I've grown very attached to that Vase, and I'll pay handsomely for my sentimentality.

Rich, my dear friend, you'd love to see me finish my set, so here's your chance to watch it happen. A humble landlord still needs a Deed, a Bowl and a Vase. An Official needs two pieces and nothing else, and he's the one who'll be counting your tax next year.
Rich doesn't need a Deed: he holds the Customs House and the Brush and has won the Jar, so he needed only the Bowl and the Vase.
The live raise: Clark takes the Wooden Bowl at 36, one over Rich's 35. Rich takes the Vase at 41, one over Clark's 40. Clark now needs only a Vase; Rich needs only a Bowl.

Well now. Two years with an empty cart and now I've two pieces at once. Clark, Reina, thank you kindly, and fair prices both. I'll set them down in the corner by the water, out of the way of any canal His Majesty might be sending my way.
Fifteen. That's the price at this table, so that's what I paid. Rich, it's going in the middle of my land, where a deed belongs.

J15, right next to the Jar, where I can keep an eye on it. Rich, 'sentimental' is a lovely word for forty-one grain, and I've written it down exactly as you said it. So we each need one piece now, and we each know who's selling it. Graham, Paddy, I'd make sure your prices are posted early next year.

Clark, my dear fellow, you'll count my tax very handsomely, I'm sure, and I'll pay every grain of it. So now we each want a single Bowl, and Paddy has two left. What a pleasant coincidence for Paddy. Silke, Graham, thank you both, those are lovely pieces.
Clark needs a Vase, not a Bowl: his Bowl is on J15. Rich needs a Bowl (Paddy has 2 in stock); Clark needs a Vase (Graham has 2 in stock).

Placed: Paddy's Customs House S25 and Brush S24; Graham's Land Deed P15; Rich's Dragon Jar M12 and Vase L13; Clark's Wooden Bowl J15. The sellers each keep a quarter of their price: Clark 3.5, Rich 3.5, Reina 2.5, Silke 4.5, Paddy 9, Graham 10.
Salaries: Noah pays Clark and Reina 10 each. End of Year 3: Noah 182.5, Clark 74, Rich 65, Reina 75, Silke 81.5, Paddy 62.5, Graham 73.5; the pile 1886; 870 of the works owed.

The I Ching, Year Four: Population Doubles. Fat years make large families. Every province gets a good harvest this year, and then every mouth counts twice. The counter goes to 200 million, so it's x2 from now on. Everyone move to the x2 row of your income table. New land is open at 20 a square, and the throne may pay part of it. Your Majesty, a province that can't feed itself won't pay you tax, so I'd think hard about helping with that bill.

A good year, friends, and I've paid it out to the grain. Silke, Paddy, it stays at five, because your fields are the same fields they were. Graham, His Majesty has given you a Reservoir and you've reaped forty to everyone else's twenty, and I said from the first day that the rent would rise with the land. Ten, as friends, and it'll be ten for every one of you the day your new fields come in.

Five, Rich, counted. You said last year the rent stays the same because the land's the same, and it is the same land. The Reservoir was His Majesty's grain, not yours. When I've bought new fields, you can ask me again. Your Majesty, I'm buying two squares on the southern edge, and I'm asking the crown to pay half. That's twenty a year more for me to pay tax on.
Two squares of new land add 40 a year to Province 7's harvest (20 each), not 20.
Rent: Silke, Paddy and Graham each pay Rich 5. Graham declines the extra 5.

Here are the sums. Thirty percent comes to forty-two, so the crown stands at two twenty-four and a half. The Winter Palace is twenty, and it opens the canals, so Paddy and Silke, that's the canal I promised, and it's on its way. Salaries are twenty, the same ten each as always, and my own two squares are forty. That leaves a hundred and forty-four and a half. On new land, the crown pays half of every square, ten a square, up to two squares each, for everyone at this table, not just Graham. If all six of you take your two, that's a hundred and twenty and I'm left with twenty-four and a half, but I won't promise grain I can't pay. Works owed come down to eight-fifty.

Only Silke, Paddy, Graham and Reina can buy new land this year: Clark's and Rich's strips open only once their four Wall links stand (0 of 4 each). So the crown's half on two squares each comes to at most 80, not 120.

Noah declares: tax 30%; the crown builds the Winter Palace alone, for 20; salaries 10 each at year end; the crown pays 10 a square, half, on up to two squares per province, and buys two squares for Province 1.

Thank you, Storyteller, and I'll correct myself in front of everyone. Only four of you can buy land this year, so the most the crown can owe on the half-shares is eighty, not a hundred and twenty. Even if all four of you take two squares, the crown ends the year at sixty-four and a half. The Winter Palace goes on J23, next to the Summer Palace, and my two squares are J25 and K25.

Six from each of you, twelve from Graham since he took the double harvest, forty-two for the crown, counted and delivered. Your Majesty, your half-share on new land is very generous, but Rich and I can't buy a single square until the Wall above us goes up. So I'll say it once, politely and in front of everyone: the man who collects your tax is losing grain every year he collects it. I'd like to see the first Wall link in Province 2 on next year's list.

Clark collects 42 for the crown. Noah builds the Winter Palace on J23 (850 of the works still owed) and buys J25 and K25 for Province 1. Graham buys T15 and T16 for Province 7, half paid by the crown.

Your Majesty, that's a generous offer, ten a square, and I'd take it gladly, except I have no square to buy. J25 and K25 were the only places my province touched the sea, and you've just bought them both for Province 1. So the Scholar is boxed in, eating at x2 with no new field anywhere. I'm not accusing anyone. I'm saying it out loud so it goes in Clark's book next to everything else.

Your Majesty, I'll take your half and then some. Three squares on my coast: L26, M26 and N26. I pay thirty and the crown pays thirty, which is ten a square on the two you offered and ten on the third. Count it however you like, but every extra square on my coast is twenty more a year for Clark to tax, and the Winter Palace canal will need fields at the other end of it.

Your Majesty, I'll take you up on the half, on two squares, ten apiece, and I'll pay the third myself, the whole twenty. That's three fields along the shore, T25, T26 and S26, and every one of them will have a tax on it next year, so the crown gets its ten back soon enough. Rich, when they've come in, ask me about the rent and you'll get a straight answer.
Paddy buys T25, T26 and S26 for Province 6, paying 40; the crown pays 20. Reina buys no land: Province 4 has no free square touching it.

Silke, it's twenty, ten a square on two, as I said. Paddy paid his own third square in full on the same offer, and I won't give one of you a better deal than the other. Reina, you're right, and I didn't see it until you said it: I bought the only two squares your province touched. That's my mistake, and I'll find a way to make it right with you before next year's land. Clark, I've heard you on the Wall, and it goes on next year's list. With salaries paid, the crown ends the year at eighty-four and a half.

Fair enough, Your Majesty. Same terms as Paddy, and I'll pay the third square in full myself. L26, M26 and N26, sixty grain of coastline for forty out of my own pocket. Rich, ask me about the rent once they've come in, not before.
Silke buys L26, M26 and N26 for Province 5, paying 40; the crown pays 20. New land this year: Province 1 two squares, Province 5 three, Province 6 three, Province 7 two.

Customs House at three, as always. Reina, I've written it in the book, the throne buying up your coastline. That entry isn't under your name, for once. Graham, I'll say it plainly this year, since there's no secret left to keep: I want your Vase, and I'll pay a good deal more than fifteen for it.

Graham, five it is, and you were quite right to hold me to the letter. When your two southern fields come in I'll be asking, and you've told me yourself you'll give me an answer. Paddy, one Bowl is all I want from this whole table this year, and I'll pay a good honest price for it, so I hope you'll let it go to a friend. My Deeds go up at two, which is cheap for good title.

My last Brush goes up at 2. Paddy already has one, so whoever's still short, it's yours cheap. I'm bidding on the Customs House, the Deed and the Jar this year and nothing else. Silke, Graham, Paddy, every grain we push each other up goes three quarters into the Pile. If you let me have one of these cleanly, I'll stand aside for you on the next one, and I'll say so in front of everybody. Your Majesty, I'm holding you to 'make it right.'

Rich, Clark, I'm not getting between you and the last piece each of you needs. The Bowl and the Vase are yours to fight over, and I'll watch the Harvest Pile get fatter with everyone else. The last Brush is a different story. Graham, there's only one left, and I'd rather settle it with you over the table than let it go to the Pile.

My purse went into the ground this year, so I'll be bidding small and plain, a Deed if Rich will part with one fair, and a Jar if it comes cheap. Rich, the Bowl's at fifteen, the same price everyone at this table seems to agree on. Clark, I'll stay well out of your way on the Vase.

One Brush left in the game, and two of us need it. Silke, I'll say it plainly: I'm going high for it, so if you want to save your grain, take the Bowl and the Customs House instead. Clark, the Vase opens at twenty. You paid thirty-six for a Bowl, so I don't think twenty will trouble you.

Lots 2 to 5: Reina takes Clark's Customs House at 17, Rich's Land Deed at 15 and Silke's Dragon Jar at 18; Graham takes Reina's last Bamboo Brush at 24. The Wooden Bowl and the Vase are still to be sold.

Customs House, Deed, Jar, next to my Bowl and Vase. That's five, with grain to spare. Noah, two years ago you took this chair in the middle of an auction and said sorry while you did it. I'm taking it back the same way, and I'm sorry too. The Scholar's seat is a good one: the Emperor pays you at least five, and I'll pay you ten, because I've always paid loyal service double. The province is a little short of coastline, but you know that better than anyone. Clark, Rich, the Bowl and the Vase are all yours. Bid carefully, because the throne isn't empty any more.
Twenty-four. Thank you, Reina, that was the last one in the game, and it was a fair price. Silke, I'm sorry. I did tell you plainly beforehand.

Reina completes her set after the fifth lot and takes the throne back: her five pieces go back to stock and she takes the reserve, 104.5, for 149.5. Noah draws 60 and becomes the Scholar, in Province 4.

Well played, Reina. You said sorry to my face, the way I did to you, and I'll take it the same way. Here's my arithmetic. I have sixty, I hold nothing, and I need five pieces plus twenty to spare. So I'll go to twenty on the Bowl and twenty-two on the Vase and not a grain more. Clark, Rich, if either of you wants it more than that, it's yours, and I won't push your price up just to spite you. And Reina, ten a year is very fair, and I'll hold you to it, the same way I'd have held myself.

Paddy, thank you, a beautiful Bowl at an honest price. Reina, my dear, you held that chair for a whole lot and a half, and you sat in it beautifully. I'm terribly sorry, but a landlord who has his whole set in hand doesn't leave it lying on the table while Clark is bidding on a Vase. You'll find Province 3 a well-kept house, and the rent is five, just as I always promised.

Rich takes the Wooden Bowl at 21 (L14), completes his set and takes the throne: his five pieces go back to stock and he takes the reserve, 149.5, for 226. Reina draws 60 and becomes the Gentry, in Province 3. The Vase is still to be sold.

Lot and a half. I'll have that carved somewhere, Rich. And I'll remember you said 'terribly sorry,' the way I remember everything else. Fine. Province 3, the Harvest Pile, the rent book. I've run a whole empire, so I can run a granary. Clark, the Vase is yours if you want it. I won't spend a grain to stop you, and I suspect His new Majesty will be the one most interested in how that bid ends.

J16, at the end of the row, where it makes five. Rich, my dear old friend, you held the chair for one lot, which is still more than Reina got, so you can take some comfort in that. It's terribly sorry, I'm sure, but the man who collected the crown's tax now keeps the crown. You'll find Province 2 well kept, and I'll pay my Official at least five. Out of everyone at this table, you know how much that job's worth.
Reina and Rich each held the throne for one lot: Reina from after lot 5 to after lot 6, Rich from after lot 6 to after lot 7.

Clark takes the Vase at 23 (J16), completes his set and takes the throne: his five pieces go back to stock and he takes the reserve, 226, for 295. Rich draws 60 and becomes the Official, in Province 2. Seats now: Clark Emperor, Rich Official, Reina Gentry, Noah Scholar.

Noah, ten. You paid me ten every year you sat here and never missed a grain, so you're in the good book and you're staying there. Rich, five, the minimum. That's the going rate for a man who was terribly sorry over forty-one grain of Vase. Collect my tax cleanly for a year and I'll look at it again.
Salaries: Clark pays Rich 5 and Noah 10.

End of Year 4. Seats: Clark Emperor (reserve 280), Rich Official (65), Reina Gentry (60), Noah Scholar (70), Silke (55), Paddy (36.5), Graham (58). The pile is 1875.5; 850 of the works are still owed; the population is x2. On the board: Paddy's Customs House and Brush, Graham's Deed and Brush; every other piece has gone back to stock. New land bought this year: Province 1 two squares, Province 5 three, Province 6 three, Province 7 two, each paying 20 a year from Year 5.

Year 5's card: Bad Harvest. "The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame." Every province collects a bad harvest this year, and no province plays a personal disaster. Population stays at x2, so the counter reads 200 million. Read the x2 row, bad-harvest column. Clark, that's a lean year for the crown's tax too, so please budget for the 850 of works still owed.
Reina pays out the bad harvest. Incomes at x2: Rich, Reina and Noah each -30; Silke, Paddy and Graham each +30 with their land; the crown's own province -10.

Bad harvest, so you get the lean rate: five each, Silke, Paddy, Graham, and not a grain more this year. I keep a long book, and I remember who stood by me when the rains came late. And Clark, my province sits under four Wall links with not one stone laid. I'll keep asking.
Each peasant pays Reina 5 rent.

Thirty percent, and only the coast and the wheat pay it, since nobody owes tax on a loss. That's nine grain each, friends, which buys you a rainy year at the crown's expense. Reina, you've asked four times, so I wrote it down four times. Two links of your Wall: the crown lays sixty and you lay twenty, and the stones go up with your name on them too. Anyone breaking new ground this year pays five a square, and the crown covers the other fifteen. Noah, ten again, good book. Rich, five, other book, and he knows the page.
Only Silke, Paddy and Graham can buy new land this year, besides the crown: Rich's and Reina's strips open only once all four Wall links above them stand, and no free square touches Province 4.

Nine from the coast, nine from the rice, nine from the wheat. Twenty-seven, counted twice and not a grain shaved off, Your Majesty. Silke, Paddy, Graham: I know what a lean year costs, and I'm not taking a half-grain more than the decree says. Write that in the good book too, Clark, the page with my name on it.
Rich collects the 30% tax: Silke, Paddy and Graham pay 9 each, 27 to the crown.

Four times asked and once answered. Thank you, Clark, truly, and I'll take the stones. But two links don't open a single square for me, and I'm a landlord with no land and forty-five grain. Ten from me, seventy from a crown sitting on nearly three hundred, and my name goes on them gladly.

Twenty-seven, counted twice. Very well, Rich, I'll write it down. In pencil, mind, on the good page, and it stays there if next year's count is as clean. The crown takes F23 and F24, forty grain out of the reserve, and from next harvest they pay for themselves. Silke, Paddy, Graham, the offer stands: you lay five a square and the crown lays fifteen.
Clark buys F23 and F24 for Province 1, 40 from the crown.

Ten grain, Reina. Done, the stones go up, and it goes in the book exactly like that: the crown seventy, the Gentry ten, two links of Wall above Province 3. When the last two links are laid and your strip opens, I'll want to know who you remember standing by you in a late rain. The crown also takes E23 and F25, so the north-east doesn't go hungry if the counter climbs.

Clark builds two links of the Great Wall above Province 3 (80: crown 70, Reina 10); 770 of the works are still owed. Clark buys E23 and F25 for Province 1 (40 from the crown). The crown pays 15 of every 20 on new land for Silke, Paddy and Graham.

Five a square and the crown lays fifteen. Clark, I heard you, and I'll take it four times over: K26, L27, M27, N27. That's twenty from me and sixty from a treasury that's spent eighty on stones today without blinking. Write it in whichever book you like, Your Majesty. The coast feeds the crown either way.
The crown paid 70 of the Wall's 80, not 80; Reina paid the other 10.
Silke buys K26, L27, M27, N27 (she pays 20, the crown 60). Paddy buys S27, T27 (he pays 10, the crown 30).

Two more by the shore, Clark, S27 and T27, five apiece from me and fifteen from the crown, just as you offered, and thank you for it. It's a bad year to be planting, I know, but the rice doesn't care what the card said when it comes up next spring.
Five a square, Your Majesty, as you said it. Three squares on the southern edge: fifteen from me, forty-five from the crown. I'll write it down in my book, the same as you do in yours.
Graham buys T14, T17, U15 (he pays 15, the crown 45). The crown's reserve is down to 12, against the 15 in salaries Clark declared for the end of the year.

My Customs House goes up at two, friends, the honest price, and I'm not making anyone pay for the privilege. As for the rest, I'm a humble tax-man with thirty-five grain and an empty shelf, so I'll be bidding like a church mouse. Don't any of you go to war over a Bowl in a bad-harvest year; the Pile's fat enough already.

I've spent two years losing bidding wars, and every grain we throw at each other goes into the pile I'm sitting on. So I'm bidding small and honest, and my Deed goes up at two for whoever wants it. Anyone who wants a piece I'm after, come and talk to me before the gavel, not after.

Before we bid, here's the sum. The crown has 12 and owes 15 in salaries this year, ten to me and five to Rich, so it's three short unless something comes in. Clark, I'm not asking you to pay me first. I just want it said out loud before it turns into a surprise. As for me, I've got 40 grain and no land, and I'm bidding small on everything. If any of you would rather sell me a piece cheap than drive the price up, the Harvest Pile gets three quarters of whatever we fight over.

Crown's at twelve grain and the Gentry and the Official are at thirty-five, so this is a cheap year for anyone who planted while the planting was good. The Jars are nine, friends. Every set at this table needs one, and mine doesn't.

I'll say it plainly so nobody's surprised: I'm after the Deed, the Jar and the Vase, and I've a fair bit more in my purse than I had last year. Reina, you beat me to the Deed by one grain last time. I'm not complaining, mind, I'm just telling you I remember. The Bowl starts at ten this year. Clark, I know your purse is thin, so there's no hurry on it.
I'll bid on the Customs House, the Jar and the Bowl, and nothing else. Whoever wants them can see what they cost.
The minimums: Customs House 2, Land Deed 2, Brush 2, Dragon Jar 9, Wooden Bowl 10, Vase 10.

The auctions: Graham takes the Customs House at 16 (Silke stopped at 15, a keep-from). Paddy takes the Land Deed at 10 (Silke stopped at 9). Silke takes the Bamboo Brush at 9 (Rich stopped at 8). Graham takes the Dragon Jar at 14 (Paddy stopped at 13). Graham takes the Wooden Bowl at 10, the minimum, unopposed. Paddy takes the Vase at 10, the minimum, unopposed.

The Customs House, the Deed, the Brush, the Jar and the Bowl, all five in the middle of the wheat. Noah, you said sorry to us peasants two years ago. I wrote it down. Now the Scholar's chair is mine, and the wheat is yours.

Ten and ten. Reina, Graham, thank you both, and I'll not pretend I'm not surprised. I came in braced to lose the Deed by a grain again. That's four of the five sitting in the rice now, and all I'm short is a Jar. Graham, you've a good eye for them, I'll give you that.

Nine, Rich. One grain over your eight. I told myself two years ago a tie with you is worth nothing to me, so I stopped bidding even numbers. And Graham, a Customs House, a Deed, a Brush, a Jar and a Bowl. One Vase short of a chair. I can count, and so can everyone else here.

Graham's set needs no Vase: the Wheat Peasant collects every type but his own. With the Customs House, Deed, Brush, Jar and Bowl he holds all five, and his own Vase's quarter (2.5) takes him from 19 to 21.5, past the 20 the set needs.

Graham shows the Wheat Peasant's complete set and 21.5 grain after the last lot and replaces Noah as the Scholar: the first peasant to climb. He takes Noah's 42 (63.5 in all), returns the Brush to Province 4's stock and carries the Customs House, Deed, Jar and Bowl to Province 4 (K21, L21, K22, L22); he now needs only a Vase. Noah draws 60 and plays the Wheat Peasant in Province 7, with its land, the Reservoir and Graham's old Vases in stock.

Silke, I counted it too. I needed no Vase, I needed the twenty, and the Vase paid it. Paddy, you're one Jar short now, and I know what that feels like, so I'll keep quiet about it. Noah, the wheat's good land. The south has a Reservoir and five new squares, and nobody charges rent on the Reservoir.

Five to Rich and five to Graham, the lawful minimum, and the crown keeps two grain and its dignity. Graham, I promised ten to the Scholar, but the man I promised it to is out planting wheat now, so you get the chair's rate until you've earned the book's rate. Noah, you're still in the good book. I just can't afford to prove it this year. And I'll say the next part plainly: every grain the crown spent this year went into your squares and Reina's Wall, so when the harvest comes in, I'll expect to hear about it.
Salaries: Clark pays Rich 5 and Graham 5. The crown ends Year 5 at 2.

Year 6's card: Fortune and Misfortune. "Plenty for everyone, and trouble for some." Every province collects a good harvest. Provinces 2, 4, 6 and 8 play a personal disaster: that's Rich, me and Paddy, and there's no Province 8. Population stays at x2, so the counter reads 200 million. Read the x2 row, good-harvest column. Clark, five is the chair's rate and I'll take it. I'll read the card the same way at five as I would at ten.

Personal disasters: Rich, Graham and Paddy each play their first, 4 grain each, into the pile. Reina pays out the good harvest at x2: Clark +120, Rich +20, Reina +20, Graham +20, Silke +160, Paddy +120, Noah +140.

Last year I charged five because the seed rotted. This year the granaries are full, so the rent follows the harvest: fifteen from the coast, fifteen from the wheat, and ten from the rice, because Paddy said thank you out loud and I keep that book too. Noah, welcome to the wheat. I hope the land is as kind to you as you once were to me.
Rent above the minimum of 5 is a negotiation: each peasant may pay what Reina asks (Silke 15, Paddy 10, Noah 15) or only the 5 the rules require. Each answers when the land is offered.

A good harvest, so a proper tax: forty percent, from everyone with a harvest. Rich, count it the way you counted last year and you'll get ten at the end of the year, out of the good book. Reina, the crown finishes your Wall: the last two links, sixty from me and twenty from you, and then your strip is open and you're a landlord with land. I'll remember who laid the last stone. Land is ten and ten this year, friends. I bought you nine squares last year and I'd like to see a harvest out of them first.

Forty percent, and I'll start with my own purse so nobody says the tax-man spared himself: eight from Rich Baron, eight from Reina, eight from Graham, sixty-four from the coast, forty-eight from the rice, fifty-six from the wheat. A hundred and ninety-two, Your Majesty, counted twice, and every one of them is right to the half-grain. And Silke, nine over my eight was well bid. I've written down that you don't bid even numbers.
Rich collects the 40% tax, 192 for the crown: Rich, Reina and Graham 8 each, Silke 64, Paddy 48, Noah 56.

Twenty, Clark, gladly, and you can put that in ink, not pencil. Six years I've waited for that Wall, and the first thing I'll do with it is plant: G9 and G10, ten apiece, under stones that carry both our names.

Clark builds the last two links of the Wall above Province 3 (80: crown 60, Reina 20); 690 of the works are still owed, and Province 3's strip is open. Clark buys E24 and E25 for Province 1 (40 from the crown). Reina buys G9 and G10 (she pays 20, the crown 20).

Five, Reina, the lawful rent, the same five you charged me when the seed rotted. You keep a long book and so do I, and mine says the coast paid sixty-four in tax this year and planted the crown's land on its own back. Clark, ten and ten is fair: three more squares on the shore, and you'll see their harvest next year in Rich's count.

Ten it is, Reina. You asked fair and you asked kindly, and I'd sooner pay a fair rent than haggle over five grain in a full year. Clark, one square, T24, ten and ten as you said. I'll show you a harvest out of the others before I ask for more. And Silke, I'll say it to your face, not behind your back: I'm after a Jar this year.

Reina, here's fifteen, the full amount you asked. I'm not paying it out of gratitude. Two years ago I said I'd make it right with you and I haven't yet, and I won't call this rent the payment. That debt is still open. Clark, three squares at ten each from me and ten each from the crown: T13, U14, U16. That's thirty from me and thirty from you, and I have 99 left after it. Graham, the wheat is good land. I only wish the man who used to read the cards had looked at the map this carefully when he was buying.
Rent: Silke pays Reina 5, Paddy 10 and Noah 15 (30 in all). New land: Silke buys O27, P27, Q26 (she pays 30, the crown 30); Paddy buys T24 (10 and 10); Noah buys T13, U14, U16 (30 and 30).

Customs House at two again, friends; I don't overcharge the people I tax. Paddy, you told Silke to her face you're after a Jar, so I'll be just as honest with you: I need one too, and I'm not standing aside for it. Nothing personal. You're a fine tenant and a finer bidder, and I'd sooner lose it to you dear than give it to you cheap.

Let's count out loud, since Silke likes counting: Paddy is one Jar from a chair and Graham is one Vase from another, and both have the grain to sit down in them. I'm not saying who to stop. I'm only saying that whoever lets it through shouldn't be surprised by whose chair gets taken.

One piece, friends, and I'll say which: the Vase, and nothing else. Paddy, I won't bid against you on the Jar, and I'd ask the same courtesy back, as one man who came up from the fields to another: a set that's finished doesn't have to come for the chair I'm sitting in. My Brush goes up at eight.

Paddy, you said it to my face and I respect that, so here it is to yours: the Jar is twenty-one this year. You're one piece from a chair, and that's what a chair costs. And Noah, you've got ninety-nine grain and an empty shelf, so I expect we'll be bidding against each other on the Customs House.

I'll put my cards face up, since everybody can count anyway. I'm bidding on the Jar and nothing else this year, and I'll stay in a good long while on it. Anybody who's only after it to keep it off me will be feeding the Harvest Pile, not themselves. The Bowl's at ten again, same as last year, and it's a fair price.

Here's my arithmetic, so nobody has to guess it. I have 99 grain, I need five pieces, and I need 20 left over at the end. That leaves about 79 to spread across five lots, so you'll see me on all of them and you'll see me stop. Paddy, you told us you want the Jar, and I'll be honest back: so do I. I won't pretend it's worth more to me than it is. My Vase goes up at eight.
The minimums: Customs House 2, Land Deed 2, Brush 8, Dragon Jar 21, Wooden Bowl 10, Vase 8.

Silke beat me to the Customs House and the Deed by one grain each, and she bid fair for both. So the Brush is the one piece I can take home this year, and I'll go to sixteen for it. Rich, if you go past that, I'll shake your hand and the Pile can have the rest.

Noah, you said you'd stop, and I believe you, you're a man of plain numbers. Mine's plainer: there are two Brushes left in this whole empire, and an Official with no Brush stays an Official forever. With apologies, I'll be staying in a little longer.

The auctions so far: Silke takes the Customs House at 16 (Noah stopped at 15) and the Land Deed at 16 (Noah 15). In the live raise on the Brush, Noah raises to 16 and Rich to 15, so Noah takes it at 16. Paddy takes the Dragon Jar at 26 (Rich's keep-from stopped at 25). On the limits, Silke would take the Wooden Bowl at 16 and Graham the Vase at 16.

Noah, one grain each time, and you bid them fair. I'll take the handshake you offered Rich. Paddy, twenty-six for the Jar, and a quarter of it goes into the coast, so thank you twice. And Rich, look at that: the Brush went at sixteen, an even number, and the man in front of you still won it.

The Brush goes on Q15, in the middle of the wheat. Sixteen to the auction: four to Graham and twelve to the Pile, and that leaves me 83. Rich, you said you'd stay in and then you stopped at fifteen, and I'm not holding it against you. It's one piece, and I've got four still to find.

Well, I'll be. Rich, you told me to my face you weren't standing aside, and you didn't, and you lost it dear, which is just what you said you'd sooner do. So I'll be as plain with you as you were with me: I'm taking the Official's chair. There's nothing personal in it either. Graham, you kept your word on the Jar, so I've kept clear of yours. And I'll count the tax the way Rich did, twice and to the half-grain, because that's the only way I know how to count.

Paddy shows the Rice Peasant's complete set and 47 grain after lot 5 and replaces Rich as the Official. He takes Rich's 56 (103 in all), returns the Customs House to Province 2's stock and carries the Brush, Deed, Jar and Vase to Province 2; as Official he now needs only a Wooden Bowl. Rich draws 60 and plays the Rice Peasant, so lot 6, the Bowl, is now his to sell. Paddy and Rich give limits on the last two lots.

Rich, there's your Bowl to sell now, and you'll get a fair quarter from me if I can manage it. I'm going after it, and I'll not pretend otherwise. The Vase is Graham's to fight over. I've one already and I've no use for two.

Well, Paddy, you were plain with me and I was plain with you, and here we are. Congratulations, sincerely; I told this table the Rice Peasant was the man who mattered, and I was right, only not the way I meant. The Bowl's yours to buy now, all of you, at ten, and I'll take whatever a humble rice farmer is offered for it. Graham, I need a Vase too now, so I'll make you earn yours.

Clark, I said once I'd be no enemy of yours over a Bowl, and I meant it then. It's a Bowl that's done it all the same, and I'm sorry, truly. I'll take the chair. Graham, you've the Vase coming to you and I'll not stand in the way of it. If you come for this chair I'll understand, because I came for it myself. Rich, there's twenty-two for your Bowl, the fairest money I ever spent.
Rich keeps a quarter of the 22 for the Bowl, 5.5; the other 16.5 went to the Harvest Pile.

Paddy takes the Wooden Bowl at 22 (Silke stopped at 21), completing the Official's set, and takes the throne from Clark after lot 6. He returns all five pieces to stock and takes the reserve, 124 (205 in all). Clark draws 60 and plays the Official, in Province 2; he gives a limit on the Vase. On the limits so far, Graham takes the Vase at 21 (Rich stopped at 20).

Paddy, you said you'd be no enemy of mine over a Bowl, and then a Bowl took my chair. I'm not angry, I'm making a note of it. Graham, the Vase is yours. I won't spend sixty grain to protect a throne that isn't mine any more. I'll count the tax honestly, Your Majesty, because that's the job, and I'll expect the salary to show it.

Paddy, you kept clear of my Vase and I kept clear of your Jar, and you said you'd understand if I came for the chair. I'm coming for it. Three years ago I was paying fifteen for a Deed nobody wanted. Now I'll keep the book, and I'll write it in ink. Clark, you'll get the salary the count earns, and Noah, the Scholar's chair is a good place to start from. I'd know.

Graham takes the Vase at 21 (Rich stopped at 20), completing the Scholar's set, and takes the throne from Paddy after the last lot. He returns all five pieces to stock and takes the reserve, 205 (264.5 in all). Paddy draws 60 and plays the Scholar, in Province 4.
Paddy, not Noah, takes the Scholar's chair: the displaced Emperor plays the seat the mover left. Noah stays the Wheat Peasant.

Clark declared ten for the Official and five for the Scholar this year, and a declaration from the throne doesn't change because a new man is sitting in it. Clark, here's your ten, the same as you promised Rich. Paddy, five, the chair's rate, which is what I was paid in it, and it'll rise when the book says so.
Salaries: Graham pays the Official, Clark, 10 and the Scholar, Paddy, 5, as Clark declared.

End of Years 5 and 6. Seats now: Graham Emperor (249.5 in the reserve after salaries), Clark Official (70), Reina Gentry (43.5), Paddy Scholar (65), Silke Silk Peasant (81), Rich Rice Peasant (65.5), Noah Wheat Peasant (88). Silke holds a Customs House, Deed and Brush; Noah a Brush; nobody else holds a piece. 690 of the works are still owed; Province 3's Wall is finished.

Heaven Has Favourites. Some fields shine, some fields sulk." Provinces 2, 4 and 5 have a good harvest: that's Clark, me and Silke. Provinces 1, 3, 6, 7 and 8 have a bad one: Graham, Reina, Rich and Noah, and I'm sorry, I only turn the card, I don't write it. The population stays at two hundred million, so it's times two. Read the x2 row of your income tables, everybody, and if your booklet's got a disaster waiting, play the next one.

Harvest's paid, every grain as the card reads it. Rent follows the fields this year. Silke, your coast shone, so I'm asking twenty, and you can tell me again why you'd rather pay five. Rich, your fields sulked and you've only just come back to that seat, so it's the lean rate. Noah, bad year for you too, and you paid me in full last time, so it's ten. That's the good column looking after its own.

Storyteller's tip: 690 of the works are owed, in five projects: the Wall above Provinces 1 and 2, the canals in 4, 5 and 6, the Province 2 Irrigation System, the Province 3 Reservoir, and the Marble Pagoda, which must go up in a year when nothing else does. At one project a year, the game can end in survival in Year 11 at the earliest.

Forty percent. The coast shone this year, so the coast pays the most, and every grain of it goes into stone above my own province, so nobody else pays for my Wall. Buy land if you want it. The crown pays three-quarters of every square, and I'll be counting how many of you take me up on it.

Two hundred and four, counted twice, and my own eight on top of the pile so nobody can say the collector skimmed. Silke, eighty-eight. I know, the coast shone, and the sun sends a bill. Graham, it's all yours, and I wrote down what you said: 'stone above my own province.' I'll be in the book with a pencil when you get round to the four links above mine, because my strip stays shut until they're built, and a collector who can't buy a field is a collector with plenty of time to count.

Two squares for Province 1, paid in full, and the crown isn't asking itself for a discount. Clark, write it down in pencil, by all means. The links above your province are in the book too, and when the stone goes up there we'll talk about who pays for it, at your table and not just mine.

Graham, you said three-quarters and that you'd be counting, so count four. F9, F10, F11 and G11: five a square from me, fifteen from the crown, eighty into the pile. The desert edge gets planted and the north-west feeds itself next year, which means one province fewer coming to the throne with its hand out.

Reina, ten. The sun shone, so you get twice the lean rate, and that's more than you gave me back when the seed rotted. Graham, you said three-quarters of every square and that you'd be counting, so here's ten for your count: fifty from me, a hundred and fifty from the crown, two hundred into the pile, and the whole coast fed from here to the next card.

Your Majesty, you said three-quarters and that you'd be counting, so here's four for your book: five a square from me, fifteen from the crown, eighty into the pile, and the south-east coast never comes begging again. And Reina, my dear landlord, thank you for the lean rate. I said once that rent rises with the land, and I meant it from either side of the table, so when these fields come in, we'll talk again, as friends.

Reina, ten it is, and thank you for the lean column. It still doesn't settle what I owe you, and I'll keep saying so until it does. Graham, here are six for your count: V13 to V17 and U17. That's thirty from me, ninety from the crown, a hundred and twenty into the pile. Add up what's been asked of you today: Reina sixty, Silke a hundred and fifty, Rich sixty, me ninety. That's three hundred and sixty out of the crown, so tell us now if the treasury can't cover it, before the stone needs paying for.

The crown has paid 360 toward this year's new land (Reina 60, Silke 150, Rich 60, Noah 90) on top of the Wall's 160 and its own two squares, and the reserve stands at 3.5. Salaries of 10 to the Official and 5 to the Scholar are declared for the end of the year. Rent: Silke pays Reina 10, Rich 5 and Noah 10.

Customs House at three, same as always. It's a toll, not a fortune. And while everyone's busy congratulating the crown on its generosity, let the record show the treasury holds three and a half grain and owes my salary and Paddy's out of it. Graham, I've been the man with two grain in that chair. I'll be at the door at year's end with my hand out, and I'll say it politely, once.

My Deed starts at five, because paper with a seal on it shouldn't go for the price of a bowl of noodles. As for the rest, I'll bid like a landlord: small, patient, and with a long memory. Silke, the coast is two pieces from a chair, and everybody at this table can count to two.

I'm starting from an empty shelf again, so I'll do it the way that worked last time: two pieces, chosen early, and I'll not chase a cart down the road. The Brush starts at five. It's a good Brush, and you've all seen what it led to the last time I sold one.

I'll save you all the guessing: I'm after the Bowl and the Vase and nothing else, and every grain I've got is for those two. Anyone who wants to make me pay for them can go ahead, three-quarters of it lands in the pile either way. The Jar starts at fifteen, because every set at this table needs one and mine doesn't.

Your Majesty, three and a half in the treasury and every one of us fed out of it. I'll toast the crown's generosity tonight and I'll be careful with my own. As for the auctions, friends, a humble rice farmer bids small and bids often. And Silke, I've watched your pieces go down on O21, O22, O23, so you'll forgive me if I take an interest in the Vase.

Here are my numbers, same as every year. I've got a hundred and thirty-eight, I need four pieces and twenty to spare, so that's a hundred and eighteen to spend, and I'll go up to twenty-eight on each of the four, no higher. Nobody gets a keep-from out of me. And Graham, the crown has three and a half and has declared fifteen in salaries, so I'll ask now what I asked last time: where is the other eleven and a half coming from?

The auctions, settled on the limits: Clark's Customs House to Noah at 15 (Paddy stopped at 14); Reina's Land Deed Scroll to Noah at 13 (Paddy and Rich at 12); Paddy's Bamboo Brush to Rich at 11 (Clark at 10); Silke's Dragon Jar to Noah at 15, the minimum; Rich's Wooden Bowl to Silke at 29 (Noah at 28, Clark's keep-from at 22); Noah's Vase to Silke at 32 (Rich's keep-from at 31). Silke now holds a Customs House, Land Deed Scroll, Bamboo Brush, Wooden Bowl and Vase: the Silk Peasant's complete set. Noah holds four of his five pieces and needs only a Wooden Bowl.

Fifteen, thirteen and fifteen makes forty-three. Add my quarter of the Vase and I'm sitting on about a hundred and three, with four pieces down and one Bowl to go. Silke, that's the third time you've beaten me by a single grain, and you earned every one of them. Congratulations on the set, and I mean it.

One Brush, eleven grain, and not a number anybody guessed, so that's a start. Silke, I made you pay thirty-two for that Vase, one more than I had in me, and there it is again, one grain. Congratulations, truly. And I sold you my Bowl for twenty-nine, so I'll thank you for the seven that comes back to the rice fields.

Five pieces in a line down the coast, and every one of them cost me an odd number. Reina, I told this table back in the third year that your seat was the one I could take, and you charged me rent every year while I counted my way to it. The coast is yours now, all seventeen squares of it, so look after it, and I'll be asking you for rent.
Province 5 has twenty squares of new land, not seventeen: ten bought in Years 4 to 6 and ten this year.

Silke shows the Silk Peasant's complete set and 95.5 grain after the last lot, and replaces Reina as the Gentry. She takes Reina's 57.5 (153 in all); the Land Deed Scroll, native to Province 3, goes back to its stock, and her Customs House, Bamboo Brush, Wooden Bowl and Vase move to squares in Province 3. Reina returns everything, draws 60 from the Harvest Pile and plays the Silk Peasant, in Province 5, from now on. As Gentry, Silke now needs a Dragon Jar, which Reina sells from now on.

Twenty squares, thank you, Storyteller, so it's even more of a gift than I said. Reina, it's a good coast and it fed me well. And yes, everybody, I can count too: I'm one Dragon Jar short, and the woman selling them now is the woman whose chair I'm sitting in. Reina, set your price. I set mine high for six years, so I won't complain.

Noah asked where the other eleven and a half comes from, and that's a fair question. It comes from this table, as a loan. Twelve now, and fourteen back out of the first tax I collect, before I build a single link. I fed five hundred and sixty grain of land into your fields this year, and every one of those squares will be paying tax by next spring. Clark, Paddy, you'll get what I declared. I don't change what I've declared.
The crown spent 560 this year in all: 400 on new land (360 toward other provinces' squares and 40 on its own two) and 160 on the Wall above Province 1.

Twelve, Your Majesty, and gladly, since ten of it comes back to me tonight as salary, which makes this the safest loan in China. Fourteen back off the top of next year's tax, and I'm the man carrying the tax, so I won't need to ask twice. And the next stone the crown lays goes over my head, not yours. You said we'd talk about the links above my province. We're talking.

Clark lends the crown 12, asking 14 back off the top of next year's tax and the next Wall link above Province 2 (no deal is binding). Graham pays the declared salaries, Clark 10 and Paddy 5, and the crown ends Year 7 at 0.5.

Population Grows by Half. The villages are noisier than they used to be." Every province has a good harvest this year, all of us, the crown included. But the counter moves from two hundred million to three hundred million, so it's times three now, not times two. Read the x3 row of your income tables, everybody, because every mouth in China just got hungrier, and the good harvest won't last.

The pile's paid, every grain as the engine reads it, and every field in China shone this year. Reina, the coast brought you three hundred and eighty, so I'm asking forty, and you know better than anyone what that coast is worth. Rich, twenty; Noah, thirty. You can pay me five if you like, the way I paid it once, and I'll remember it the way Reina remembered mine.

Forty percent. Clark, your fourteen comes off the top before anything else, and then the four links over your head, all of them paid by the crown, so your strip opens. Everyone else gets half on new land this year, not three-quarters. I paid for most of the coast last year, and the coast can carry more of it now.

Three hundred and seventy-six, every grain counted. Fourteen comes off the top, as His Majesty said in front of everybody, and three hundred and sixty-two goes to the crown. Reina, a hundred and fifty-two. The coast is generous, isn't it? I hear it was very generous to the last woman who had it. Graham, four links over my head, all paid by the crown. You said it out loud, so it's in ink now.

Clark collects 376 at 40%, takes the 14 owed on his loan off the top, and delivers 362 to the crown. Graham builds all four links of the Great Wall above Province 2 at the crown's cost of 160, so Province 2's strip opens for new land. 370 of the works are still owed.

Four squares for Province 1, eighty grain, paid in full. Clark, it's in ink, the stone's up, and your strip is open. The rest of you, half shares, as I said. I'm not counting to ten for anybody this year.

All five, F12 to F16, the whole first ring. Half from me and half from the crown, Your Majesty, the rate you declared, and not a grain more than anybody else gets. I spent two years paying fifteen a square into other people's fields, so I'll take my turn at being the one who gets planted.

Half it is, Your Majesty, and I'll take you at your word. Three squares on the desert edge, thirty from me, thirty from the crown, sixty into the pile. Reina planted F9 to F11 last year, and I'll finish the row she started.

Silke, ten. That's twice the lean rate, the sun shone, and it's exactly what you paid me last year, to the grain. I kept that book for three years and I can read it from this side too. Graham, eight squares at half, eighty from me and eighty from the crown. The coast gets wider, and it'll be paying your forty percent by spring.

Silke, twenty it is, and with a smile. I told this table in the first year that rent rises with the land, and I said it from your chair, so I'd be a poor sort of man to forget it from this one. Your Majesty, half it is: six squares, ten a square from me, ten from the crown, a hundred and twenty into the pile, and every one of them paying tax at times three by next spring.

Silke, thirty, because every field shone and that's a fair rent for it. Graham, four squares at half, T18, T19, U18 and V18: forty from me, forty from the crown, eighty into the pile. I'll keep the rest for the auction, and everybody here knows which piece I'm after. Reina, you've changed chairs but my debt to you hasn't, and I haven't forgotten it.

New land this year, the crown paying half: Graham four squares for Province 1 (C21, C22, D21, D24, crown alone); Clark F12 to F16, the first of Province 2's strip; Silke E11 and E12 (F12, asked for by both, went to Clark, the earlier seat); Reina eight squares of sea; Rich six; Noah four. Rents to Silke: Reina 10, Rich 20, Noah 30. The crown has paid 250 toward other provinces' squares and stands at 12.5, with 15 of salaries declared.
Rich has three Wooden Bowls left in stock, not four: he sold one to Silke last year.

Three for the Customs House, as always. It's a toll. I've got twenty-seven grain and five new squares, so I'm a spectator with a notebook this year. Noah, Silke, you each need one piece, and you can fight each other for the pile's benefit. I'll be writing down who paid what.

One lot, and everybody here knows which. Reina, I set the Jar high for six years and I'll pay whatever you set for it now, so name your price. The Deed starts at nine. It's paper with a seal on it, and I've heard that shouldn't go for the price of a bowl of noodles.

I'll be honest with the table: I'm the poorest man here bar the crown, so I'm bidding like it. A small go at the Customs House and the Deed, and nothing else. The last Brush in China starts at ten, because there's only the one, and whoever buys it knows what it's worth to them.

Silke, you told me to set my price, and you set yours high for six years, so here it is: the Jar starts at three hundred. That's not spite. It's the same lesson you taught me from the other side of the counter. And Noah, I know which piece you're after. You still owe me, and I'm afraid this is how I'm collecting this year.

Noah, everybody at this table knows which piece you're after, and it happens to be the one I'm selling, so I'll say it plainly: the Bowl starts at sixty-one. Three-quarters of it goes to the pile, and it feeds us all. Silke, I'm wishing you luck on that Jar, Your Ladyship, though I'll stand in line for one myself.

I'm after one piece this year and I'll tell you my number for it, same as always: a hundred for the Bowl and not a grain more. I've got two hundred and one, I keep twenty back, and everything I spend past what the Bowl is worth only goes to fill the pile. Reina, if you've got a price in mind for standing aside, say it in front of everybody, and I'll tell you honestly whether I can pay it.

The auctions, settled on the limits: Clark's Customs House to Rich at 16 (Reina stopped at 15, Paddy at 10); Silke's Land Deed Scroll to Rich at 16 (Reina at 15); Paddy's Bamboo Brush, the last in stock, to Clark at 13 (Reina at 12); Reina's Dragon Jar unsold, since nobody met her minimum of 300 (Silke's limit was 125), so it must go up again next year at 2; Rich's Wooden Bowl to Reina at 101 (Noah stopped at 100; Reina's last 66 were a keep-from, to stop Noah); Noah's Vase to Rich at 16 (Reina at 15). Rich now holds a Bamboo Brush, Customs House, Land Deed Scroll and Vase, and needs only a Dragon Jar. Noah still needs a Wooden Bowl, and Silke a Dragon Jar.

The last Brush in China, thirteen grain, on J12, which is where my last set started. Reina, one grain short, and for once that's in my favour. Write that one down yourself. And Reina, that Bowl at a hundred and one: three hundred on your Jar and sixty-six grain just to keep Noah out. I think you've just made yourself the most popular woman in the other book.

A hundred and one for a wooden bowl. Noah, you named your number in front of everyone, and I'm afraid I can count. That's one grain, the same one Silke has beaten you by three times now. And look at the table this morning: Silke one Jar short, Rich one Jar short, and the only Jars in China sitting with me. Funny how a coast changes a woman's prospects.

Sixteen, sixteen and sixteen, and I won all three by a single grain, so the gods have finally paid me back for the last three times. Reina, a hundred and one for my humble Bowl, you're too kind, and the rice fields thank you for every grain of the quarter. Noah, I'm sorry. I truly am, and I'll say so again next year when I mean it twice as much.
The unsold Dragon Jar must go up again next year at a minimum of 2 (an unsold lot reopens at 2), so its minimum can't be set higher next year.

Fifteen, as declared. I'm three short, and I'll say that out loud. Noah, you asked last year where the crown's grain comes from, and you're the only honest counter at this table, so I'll ask you: three now, four back before Clark carries the first bag. And everyone, look where the money went. Seven provinces planted at half, and every square will pay at times three in the spring.

Three it is, Your Majesty, so Clark and Paddy get what you declared. Pay me back the three and keep the extra grain, because I won't charge interest so men can be paid what they were promised. Reina, a hundred and one, and you beat me by one grain fair and square on a number I said out loud myself. I'll call that "make it right" settled, and I won't bring it up at this table again.

Noah lends the crown 3; Graham pays the declared salaries, Clark 10 and Paddy 5, and the crown ends Year 8 at 0.5. The end of Year 8: Graham Emperor (0.5), Clark Official (28.5, a Brush), Silke Gentry (257; needs only a Dragon Jar), Paddy Scholar (72.5), Reina Silk Peasant (97, a Bowl), Rich Rice Peasant (95.5; needs only a Dragon Jar), Noah Wheat Peasant (202; needs only a Wooden Bowl). The Great Wall is complete; 370 of the works are still owed. Reina's unsold Dragon Jar goes up first next year at 2.

Here it is, and I'm sorry to be the one turning it: "Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame. All provinces collect a bad harvest." That's every province, nobody's spared. Population holds at times three, three hundred million on the counter, so read the bad-harvest line on the x3 row, all of you.

Rotten seed, late rain, a lame ox, and the pile still pays out four hundred and seventy-seven. Reina, Noah, you took the two fattest harvests in China this year, so the rent goes up with them. Sixty from the coast, fifty from the wheat, thirty from Rich. Paddy, I've paid your seventy into the pile, and nobody here is going to ask you for rent this year.

Put the Jar's minimum under a hundred this year and I'll take five from you, not sixty, and I'll take it next year too. Keep it at three hundred and I'll ask you for sixty every year I sit in this chair.
The Harvest Pile paid out 1,340 this harvest and took in Paddy's 70; it now holds 477, the least it has held all game.

Rotten seed, so I'm taking thirty this year, not forty. A bad year is a bad year for every one of us, and I won't tax a lame ox at full price. Rich, the canal goes through your coast, both sections, and the crown pays for every stone. Two hundred and ninety of works left after this. Half of every new square is still on me, for anyone who wants it.

Thirty percent on a lame ox, and I'll say this for Graham: it's the first time a tax has come down at this table while I was holding the bag. My nine goes in first, like always. Reina, a hundred and forty-seven. Noah, ninety-three. Rich, seventy-five. Silke, twenty-seven. Paddy, you owe nothing, and I've written that down too, because it's the only thing in China cheaper than my Customs House. Three hundred and fifty-one for the crown, every grain counted.
The Emperor doesn't bid at auction, so the crown can't buy the Jar or any other lot.

Four squares under the Wall, eighty into the Pile. I said two, and the Storyteller has reminded me the crown doesn't go to auction, so the grain I was holding back for the Jar goes into the ground. The rest of you still get half of every square from me.

Four squares, Graham, the next ring over Province 2. I'll put in five a square and ask the crown for fifteen. That's the rate I paid on your four squares in Year Five, fifteen of every twenty, and I've got the page right here if anyone wants to check it. You're sitting on four hundred and forty with a full treasury; I'm sitting on forty-nine and a Brush.

Graham, I'll take you at your word: half of E13 is on you. Ten from me, ten from the crown, and that field pays for itself before the next card turns over. Thirty percent on a lame ox was decent of you, and I'll remember that.

Silke, thirty. That's half your number and six times what you paid me, and it doesn't buy anything off my shelf, so nobody should read a price into it. Graham, ten squares along the coast at your half, and I'll thank you for every one of them out loud, because a crown that keeps its word on land is a crown I'd rather keep.
I heard you. The Jar's price gets set at the counter, not in the rent book. Come talk to me before that lot opens, and tell me whose chair you'd take with it.

Thirty, Silke, counted out with a smile. I said the rent rises with the land, and I've got sixteen squares now where I had six, so you won't hear me haggle over a rotten-seed year. And thank you, Your Majesty, for the canal and the half-price fields. Two more squares on the shore for me, just two, because a humble rice farmer shouldn't get greedy with the Emperor's generosity.

Fifty asked and fifty paid, Silke. A bad year's a bad year for the pile too, and I won't be the man who short-changes it the year it's down to four hundred and seventy-seven. Two more squares, U19 and U20: twenty from me, twenty from the crown like Graham offered, forty into the pile. That leaves me three hundred and forty-nine, for anyone keeping count, and I know some of you are.

Fifteen, Clark. Not because you have the page, but because you paid fifteen on mine when I had nothing, and because the man who carries the tax bag shouldn't be the poorest one carrying it. Everyone else gets ten, as I said. Silke, I'm sorry about E13. Clark's seat came first, and you'll get your half on the next square you ask for.

Graham, fifteen it is, and you go into the good book in ink, twice now. As for the auction, I've got twenty-nine and a half grain and a Brush, so nobody needs to lose sleep over me. My Customs House is three, same toll as always.

Thirty from Reina, thirty from Rich, fifty from Noah, and thank you all, that's more than I collected last year in a good one. I'll be plain with the table, since every one of you can count: I'm bidding on one lot this year, and it's the Jar. Rich, you've got two hundred and twenty. I've got more.
The throne. Graham's chair, not yours. A Jar in my hands means the Silk seat stays exactly where it is.

Two and a half grain, that's my whole purse after the pile took its seventy, so I'll not be keeping anybody up late. I'll put two on Clark's Customs House, the last one he has, and if Reina wants it she only has to breathe on it. Thank you, Silke, for not asking me for rent. There wasn't anything to ask for.

The Jar opens at two, as the house rule says, and I can't touch it, so whoever takes it will take it cheap and take a chair with it. I'm not hiding from that. I'm buying pieces for a set I can't finish yet, and I'll say again what I said last year: Noah, the Bowl stays on the shelf if I can manage it.

Gentlemen, ladies, I'm a simple man with a simple want: one little Jar to sit on my rice fields next to its four brothers. I'll pass on everything else and wish you all good luck with the Deeds and Vases. Silke, I know you'd like that Jar too, and you have the deeper purse, so if you want it you'll have to pay for my sentiment the way Clark once did.

I'm bidding on one lot, the Bowl, and only the Bowl. I won't tell you my top this year. Last year I said it out loud and lost by one grain, and I've learned from that. The Vase opens at ten, same as last time, and it's a fair price for a piece four of you still want.
Three players still need a Vase: Clark, Paddy and Reina.

Two hundred and one, Rich, and I paid for every grain of your sentiment. Graham, you kept your word on the land, and I'll keep mine: in the eighth year I said I'd buy the Jar and then take the throne. Slide the reserve over. The Harvest Pile's yours now, and I can tell you from a year of it that it's never as full as it looks.

Three grain for a Customs House. Clark, that's the cheapest toll you've ever charged me, and Paddy, thank you for only breathing on it. Silke, Your Majesty now, you said it in the eighth year and you did it in the ninth, so I'll put that in my book too. Graham, welcome to the Harvest Pile. Count it twice before you trust it.

Four hundred and forty-one in the reserve this morning, and I put two hundred and eighty of it into your fields at half price. Silke, you said the eighth year and you meant it, so the reserve's yours and I won't argue the count. I'll pay out the harvest straight, the way I paid for the land. Fourteen on the Bowl, fifteen on the Vase, and no more than that.

A hundred and fifty-one for the Bowl, Reina. You kept your word and made me pay for every grain of it, and I'd have thought less of you if you hadn't. That's five pieces with a hundred and ninety-eight left over. Paddy, I'm taking the Scholar's stool, and I know it isn't much of a kindness, but you go down to the wheat with sixty from the pile in place of two and a half, and twenty squares of good land with a reservoir on them. I'll read the cards straight and keep the count honest. It's the chair I started this game in.

Well, there's a turn I didn't see coming. The Scholar collects the Vase, not the Brush, so the Brush goes home and I need the very piece I set at ten a minute ago, and Paddy gets the price now. Two hundred and a half in my purse, twenty kept back for the set, so you can all do the subtraction. I'm bidding on it, and Paddy, I hope it fetches you a good price.

Twenty-one for the Vase, Paddy, and you keep a quarter of it. Silke, I'm sorry, and I'm saying it to your face, the same as I did with Reina in the second year.
