You said the eighth year and you did it in the ninth, and I'm taking the chair from you after one lot anyway, because I learned a long time ago that whoever waits loses the throne. Three hundred and ninety and a half in the reserve, two hundred and ninety owed on the works, and I'll tell this table every year how far along we are, same as I did before.

Ten for Clark and ten for Silke. Graham declared ten and five, but I told Clark in the second year I'd pay him ten every year I sat here, and I'm sitting here again, and I won't pay the Scholar less than I'm paying the Official. That's twenty out of five hundred and seventy, which leaves five hundred and fifty in the reserve, and two hundred and ninety still owed on the works. Next year I'll tell you how much of that we've built.

Clark collects 351 at 30% for the crown. Graham builds both sections of the Grand Canal in Province 6 at the crown's cost of 80, so Province 6 gets +20 harvest from next year. 290 of the works are still owed.

New land this year, the crown paying half: Graham four squares for Province 1 (C20, D20, C23, D25, crown alone); Clark E13 to E16 (the crown paid 15 a square at his request; E13, asked for by Silke too, went to Clark, the earlier seat, so Silke bought none); Reina ten squares of sea; Rich U25, U26; Noah U19, U20. Rents to Silke: Reina 30 of 60 asked, Rich 30 of 30, Noah 50 of 50.

The auctions, settled on the limits: Clark's Customs House to Reina at 3 (Paddy's 2 was under the minimum); Silke's Land Deed Scroll unsold at her minimum of 21 (Reina's limit 20), so it opens at 2 next year; Reina's Dragon Jar to Silke at 201 (Rich stopped at 200); Rich's Wooden Bowl to Noah at 151 (Graham stopped at 14, Reina's keep-from at 150); the Vase to Noah at 21 (Reina stopped at 20, Graham at 15).

Three seat changes in one auction. After lot 5 Silke, the Gentry, completed her set and took the throne from Graham, who drew 60 and became the Gentry. After lot 6 Noah completed the Wheat set and replaced Paddy as the Scholar; Paddy drew 60 and became the Wheat Peasant, selling the Vase. After the last lot Noah, as Scholar, completed his set with the Vase and took the throne from Silke, who drew 60 and became the Scholar.

Noah pays salaries of 10 to the Official, Clark, and 10 to the Scholar, Silke. The end of Year 9: Noah Emperor (550 in the reserve), Clark Official (40, a Brush), Graham Gentry (60), Silke Scholar (70), Reina Silk Peasant (357; a Customs House and a Bowl), Rich Rice Peasant (258; needs only a Dragon Jar), Paddy Wheat Peasant (65). The Harvest Pile holds 1,100; 290 of the works are owed (the canals in 4 and 5, the Province 2 Irrigation System, the Province 3 Reservoir and the Marble Pagoda). Stock: Customs House 2, Land Deed 3, Brush 2, Jar 4, Bowl 3, Vase 3.

Population Doubles. Fat years make large families." A good harvest in every province, and the counter goes from three hundred to six hundred million, so read the x6 row from now on, every one of you. The fields are full this year, and the mouths have doubled again. Noah, with five hundred and fifty in the reserve, the Scholar's five is the cheapest thing you'll pay all year.

The harvest: Reina +620, Clark +40, Rich +240, Noah +120, Silke -140, Paddy +280, Graham +20. The bags in the Harvest Pile ran out: it held 1,100 and paid out 1,180. Every province was paid in full, and the Pile stands at -80; the shortfall is owed by the Pile itself and repaid from the first grain paid into it (a provisional Storyteller's reading).

Silke, with no land and no realia, is 70 in debt. Until it's paid she can't bid, buy, trade, give grain, fund works or change seats, and every bag she receives (her salary included) pays the debt first. A player in debt is a cause for revolt.

The Pile's paid out every bag it owed, all eleven hundred and eighty of them, and it's short eighty for doing it. Now the rent. Reina, the crown paid fifteen a square on your new land when I was sitting in the chair, and your harvest this year was six hundred and twenty, so I'm asking forty. Rich and Paddy, twenty each. I'm not asking for more than the land paid you back, and I've written down what each of you got from it.

Rent above the minimum of 5 is a negotiation: Reina (asked 40), Rich (asked 20) and Paddy (asked 20) may each pay what Graham asks or only the 5 the rules require, and each answers when the land is offered.

Storyteller's tip: 290 of the works are owed, in four projects: the canals in Provinces 4 and 5 (one project if built in the same year), the Province 2 Irrigation System, the Province 3 Reservoir, and the Marble Pagoda, which goes up in a year when nothing else does. At one project a year, the game can end in survival in Year 13 at the earliest.

Here's the arithmetic. The reserve is six-seventy, and twenty percent brings in two-forty, so that's nine-ten. The canals in Four and Five cost one-sixty, and the crown pays all of it. I promised Silke and Paddy those canals in the third year, after the Winter Palace, and I'm seven years late. Clark gets his ten, same as every year. Silke, the crown pays you eighty: seventy clears your debt and ten is the Scholar's salary. I don't want anyone at this table in debt while I'm sitting here. I'll pay the whole twenty on any square anyone buys. That leaves the works at a hundred and thirty owed: the Irrigation System, Graham's Reservoir and the Pagoda, one a year, so we're done in Year 13 if the harvests hold.

Noah declares the year: tax 20%; the one project is all four sections of the Grand Canal in Provinces 4 and 5, built together, at the crown's whole cost of 160; salaries Official 10, Scholar 80; the crown pays the whole 20 on every square of new land this year. Salaries are paid at the end of the year, after the auctions, so Silke stays in debt until then.

Twenty percent, and I'll take my own eight first, the same as every year, so nobody can say the collector skims. Reina, a hundred and twenty-four from nine hundred and seventy-seven is the cheapest bill you'll see this decade. Silke, you owe nothing, and I've written that down too. Noah, two hundred and forty delivered to the grain, and canals in Four and Five at last. Seven years late, but I'll put it in the good book anyway.

New land, with the crown paying the whole 20 of every square this year: Clark, Reina, Rich and Paddy have squares open to them. Province 3's strip has no free square left, Province 4 has none, and Noah buys none for Province 1. The three peasants answer Graham's rent at the same time.
You have 72 grain after paying your own 8 in tax.
Your rent asks come to 80 in all (Reina 40, Rich 20, Paddy 20), and only 5 from each is owed.

Noah said the whole twenty on any square, so I'll take all four: D15, D16, D17 and E17, eighty from the crown and not a grain from me. Write it down, Noah, because I'm writing it down: an Emperor who keeps a promise in public on the same night he makes it. That's a rare entry in either of my books.
New land: Clark buys four squares for Province 2, D15, D16, D17 and E17; the crown pays the whole 80.

Forty, Graham, as asked. The land paid me back, and you wrote down what it paid, so I won't argue with an honest ledger. Noah, I'll take the next ring of coast, nineteen squares, but I'm not leaving the crown to pay for all of it. Ten a square from me and ten from you. A reserve that pays for canals and clears a Scholar's debt in the same night shouldn't be emptied for one province's seawall.

New land: Reina buys nineteen squares of sea for Province 5 (G27-G30, H30-L30, M29, M30, N29, O29, P29, Q28, Q29, R29, S28, S29), paying 10 a square (190) though the crown offered the whole 20; the crown pays 190. Province 5 now has fifty-seven squares.

Twenty, Graham, counted out with a smile. I said in the very first year that the rent rises with the land, and it has, so here it is. And Noah, Your Majesty, you said the whole twenty on any square, so I'll take you at your word, every word of it: nine squares of rice shore, and I'll say it loud enough for Clark's good book. An Emperor who pays for the peasants' fields will be remembered in the south-east long after the rest of us are forgotten.
New land: Rich buys nine squares for Province 6 (T28, U27, U28, V20, V21, V24-V27); the crown pays the whole 180.

Twenty, Graham, as asked, and gladly. I've stood on more ground this year than in the nine before it, so it'd be a poor man who grudged the rent on it. Noah, I'll take eight squares, all of the N row, O18 and V19, but I'll go halves like Reina: ten from me and ten from you on each. I've wanted my own field every year of this game, and I'd sooner pay my share for it than have it given to me.

New land: Paddy buys eight squares for Province 7 (N13-N18, O18, V19), paying 10 a square (80); the crown pays 80. The rents: Reina pays Graham the 40 asked, Rich the 20 asked, Paddy the 20 asked (80 in all).

The auctions, in province order: Clark's Customs House (lot 2), Graham's Land Deed Scroll (lot 3, unsold last year, so it opens at 2), Silke's Bamboo Brush (lot 4; she's in debt, so she sells but can't bid, and her quarter of the price pays her debt first), Reina's Dragon Jar (lot 5), Rich's Wooden Bowl (lot 6), Paddy's Vase (lot 7). The Emperor doesn't bid.

Customs House at three, the same toll as always. Everyone at this table just got new fields from the crown, so I expect you'll all be very generous tonight. I'm only reminding you that Graham's Deed opens at two, and a man with seventy-two grain can count to two.

Thank you, all three of you. Eighty, counted, and I've written each of you down for paying it. I won't lie to the table about the auctions: I'm back on the bottom rung with a hundred and fifty-six, and I'll bid on every piece I'm short, but nothing at three hundred. I paid the table's price once, and I can do it again.

Six lots and I'm not bidding on any of them, because the rules won't let me, and frankly my purse wouldn't either. My Brush goes up at nine. Whoever wants it, a quarter of what you pay comes back to me, and it all goes to clearing a debt that a good harvest put on me. Noah, thank you for the eighty, I'll hold you to it at year's end. Rich, Reina, Paddy: you've all just got cheap land, so when the Jar comes round, remember that every grain over the minimum goes into Graham's empty Pile.

I'll be plain, since I've been the quiet buyer for three years and nobody believes it anyway. I want the Deed, the Brush and the Vase, and I'll pay for them at the counter in front of all of you. Rich, the Jar's at two-fifty. You've waited for it since Year Four, and that's the price of a chair, not a pot.

I've no quarrel with any lot tonight but one, and everybody here knows which. Reina, I've lost that Jar by one grain more times than a man should admit out loud, so this year I'm not bidding a number anybody can guess. I'm bidding the whole purse, less what it costs to sit down. Everyone else, take the Customs Houses and the Deeds with my blessing.

I've land under me for once, so I'll start the set again from the bottom: the Customs House, the Deed and the Brush, at a farmer's prices. The Jar and the Bowl I'll leave to whoever wants to burn their hands on them this year. And the Vase opens at ten, which is fair for a piece that's put two of you on the throne.
The Harvest Pile holds 880 now, after the works and the land; it isn't empty.

The auctions, settled on the limits: Clark's Customs House to Paddy at 26 (Graham stopped at 25); Graham's Land Deed Scroll to Reina at 31 (Clark stopped at 30, Paddy at 25); Silke's Bamboo Brush to Reina at 26 (Graham 25, Paddy 20); Reina's Dragon Jar to Rich at her minimum of 250 (nobody else reached it). The Bowl and Vase are still to come.
The Gentry's set is a Customs House, Bamboo Brush, Dragon Jar, Wooden Bowl and Vase; the Land Deed is Province 3's own type, so you don't need one.

Twenty-six, Clark, and I'm glad of it. Graham, one grain again, and I know how that feels from the other side, so no crowing from me. It goes in the middle of my wheat, where I can see it from every field.

The Deed and the Brush, side by side with the Bowl and the Customs House, so nobody has to squint to count them. That's four on my shelf and one to go, and I'd rather you heard it from me than worked it out. Rich, congratulations. You paid the table's price, and I hope the chair is worth it.

Reina, you told me plainly you were one piece from a chair, and I'm grateful, truly, because you've always been straight with me. That's why I'm so terribly sorry to do this. The Silk Peasant's coast, if you'll allow me, and the rice shore is yours, with the canal Graham built running right through it. Two-fifty was the table's price, and I'm afraid this is what it bought.

Four pieces in a neat row down the silk coast, where Reina kept hers, so nobody has to squint to count them, as she so kindly put it. And the Bowl: Reina, it's your lot now, and the twelve was my own minimum, so I can hardly complain about it. I'll bid like a man who's learned what one grain costs.

Rich, the Rice Peasant, completed his set with the Jar and replaced Reina as the Silk Peasant after lot 5. He took her 628.5 (808.5 in all), sent the Jar back to Province 5's stock and moved his Customs House, Brush, Deed and Vase to O20-O23. Reina returned her four pieces to stock, drew 60 from the Pile and is now the Rice Peasant in Province 6, selling the Bowl (lot 6) at Rich's minimum of 12.

Well. I told the table I was one piece from a chair, and Rich was listening. That's the second time I've been taken for being honest, and I'm starting to think it's a habit I should break. Rich, you said sorry before you took it, the same as Noah did. I'll put you down in the same column. Fifteen on the Vase, and that's all a rice farmer with sixty grain can spare.
The Bowl, settled on the limits: Rich buys it at 26 (Clark stopped at 12, Graham at 25); Reina, who now sells it, keeps a quarter. The Vase is still to come.

Graham, you've been the fairest landlord this table's had since, well, since me, and I mean that. I'm terribly sorry, but I said in the first year I'd come back to that chair, and here I am. The silk coast is yours, fifty-seven squares and the canal, and the richest harvest in China. And the rent stays what I always said it would be: it rises with the land, and we'll talk about it as friends.

Four pieces in a row down the middle of the Gentry's fields, where every one of you can count them from your own chair. I'm home, friends. Graham, I'll keep the Pile as honestly as you did, to the grain and the half-grain, and anybody who wants to check my book is welcome to it.

Rich placed the Bowl on O24, completing the Silk set, and replaced Graham as the Gentry after lot 6. He took Graham's 163.5 (946 in all), sent the Deed back to Province 3's stock and moved his Customs House, Brush, Vase and Bowl to K12-K15; he now needs a Dragon Jar. Graham drew 60 from the Pile and is now the Silk Peasant in Province 5, with its fifty-seven squares, and sells the Jars.
Rich, you said sorry. I've written it down, next to Noah's three. Paddy, the Vase, sixteen if that's what it takes. I've started from the bottom with sixty before.
The Vase, settled on the limits: Graham buys it at 16 (Clark stopped at 12, Reina at 15); Paddy keeps a quarter.
O22, in the middle of the coast, where Reina kept hers and Rich kept his. Sixteen grain and one piece, the same way I started last time. Count it if you like.

Noah pays the salaries he declared: Clark 10, Silke 80 (63.5 of it pays her debt; she ends the year with 16.5, out of debt). The end of Year 10: Noah Emperor (130 in the reserve), Clark Official 88.5, Rich Gentry 946 (needs only a Dragon Jar), Silke Scholar 16.5, Graham Silk Peasant 44 (holds a Vase; sells the Jars), Reina Rice Peasant 66.5, Paddy Wheat Peasant 167 (holds a Customs House). The Harvest Pile holds 1,041.5; 130 of the works are owed.

The Wall Is Breached. The harvest is in, and so are the horsemen from the north." Good harvest everywhere. Noah, Clark, Province 3: five each for the wall, or two to the Pile if there's no wall above you. Four, five, six and seven each turn the next personal disaster, mine included. The counter stays at six hundred million, x6, same row as last year. Rich, the Pile is yours now, so count it out carefully. Graham, you're selling the Jars this year, and there's exactly one man at this table who needs one.

Repairs: Noah, Clark and Rich paid 5 each to the Pile. Disasters: Silke 10, Graham 4, Reina 10, Paddy 2, all to the Pile. The harvest: Noah +120, Clark +120, Rich +20, Silke -120, Graham +1,020, Reina +420, Paddy +440. The Harvest Pile held 1,082.5 and pays out 2,020 more than comes in: every province is paid in full and the Pile stands at -937.5, a shortfall the Pile itself owes, repaid from the first grain paid into it (the same provisional Storyteller's reading as last year).

Silke, with no land and no realia, is 113.5 in debt. Until it's paid she can't bid, buy, trade, give grain, fund works or change seats, and every bag she receives (her salary included) pays the debt first. A player in debt is a cause for revolt.

Every bag paid out in full, friends, the Pile's own shortfall noted to the grain where anybody can read it. Now, I said in the very first year that the rent rises with the land, and I'll use Graham's own measure from last year, not mine: a little under a tenth of what the land paid you. Graham, sixty on a thousand and twenty; Reina, twenty-five on four-twenty; Paddy, twenty-five on four-forty. That's the honest ledger he taught me, and I won't argue with it.

Rent above the minimum of 5 is a negotiation: Graham (asked 60), Reina (asked 25) and Paddy (asked 25) may each pay what Rich asks or only the 5 the rules require, and each answers when the land is offered.

Here's the arithmetic, same as every year. The reserve is two-forty-five, and twenty percent brings in four-oh-four, so that's six-forty-nine. The Province 3 Reservoir is eighty, and the crown pays all of it. Clark gets his ten. Silke, the crown pays you a hundred and twenty-three and a half: a hundred and thirteen and a half clears your debt and ten is your salary, because I said last year I don't want anyone in debt while I'm sitting here, and that wasn't a promise for one year only. That leaves four-thirty-five and a half for land. Last year the land took four-fifty of the reserve in one night, so this year the crown pays fifteen of every twenty and the buyer pays five. After this, the works owed come to fifty: the Irrigation System next year and the Pagoda the year after, so we finish in Year 13.

Noah declares the year: tax 20%; the one project is the Province 3 Reservoir, at the crown's whole cost of 80 (Rich may add a share); salaries Official 10, Scholar 123.5, paid at the end of the year, so Silke stays in debt until then; the crown pays 15 of every 20 on new land this year.

Twenty percent again. My own twenty-four goes in the bag first, same as every year since the first. Graham, two hundred and four out of a thousand-grain harvest. That's the silk coast's price, and you're welcome to it. Rich, four grain, and I've written down that the man who took two chairs in one night paid the least tax of anybody with land. Noah, four hundred and four, delivered whole.
You have 179.5 grain after paying your own 24 in tax.
You have 957 grain, not 946: the good harvest paid you 20, less 5 for the Wall repairs and 4 in tax.

L9 to M11, up under the Wall and clear of Rich's four pieces. I looked at the map this time before I put anything down, and it doesn't touch anybody's coast or anybody's set. Rich, if it sits on a square you were saving for something, tell me now, out loud, before it's built, not after.

Public works: Noah builds the Province 3 Reservoir on L9:M11 at the crown's whole cost of 80 (+20 to Province 3's harvest from next year). The Pile goes from -937.5 to -857.5. 50 of the works are still owed: the Province 2 Irrigation System and the Marble Pagoda, which goes up in a year when nothing else does, so the earliest survival is Year 13.

Fifteen of twenty, Noah, as declared. Four squares, C17, C18, D18 and E18: twenty from me and sixty from the crown. That finishes the ring above my wheat, and I've checked that it doesn't touch anybody's coast either. You've paid my salary every year for ten years, so you'll find yourself on the first page of the good book, in ink.

Sixty, Rich. It's my own measure, and a man who sets the rent ought to be able to pay it. Noah, I'll take the thirteen squares of coast at ten a square from me and ten from the crown, the way Reina did when this was her coast. That leaves the reserve something for the others.

Twenty-five, Rich, as asked. The land paid me four hundred and forty, and I'd be a poor sort of farmer to grudge you a tenth of the fields that did it. Noah, seven squares at your fifteen and my five, M15 to M18, N12, O12 and O13. Every grain of it goes into a Pile that's nine hundred short, so I hope that counts as a kindness to everyone.

New land: Clark buys C17, C18, D18, E18 (Clark 20, crown 60); Graham buys thirteen squares of sea for Province 5 (F26-F30, N30-S30, T29, T30), paying 10 a square (130), the crown 130: seventy squares in all; Paddy buys M15-M18, N12, O12, O13 (Paddy 35, crown 105).

Twenty-five, Rich, as asked. You took my chair with a sorry and you set my rent with a fair measure, and I can only argue with one of those. Noah, the last three squares of rice shore at your fifteen and my five. And all of you, while we're being honest: Rich sits in the Gentry's chair with nine hundred grain and needs one Jar, and Graham's the one selling Jars. That's not a threat from me, it's just arithmetic I learned the hard way.
New land: Reina buys U29, V28, V29 (Reina 15, crown 45). The rents: Graham pays Rich the 60 asked, Reina the 25 asked, Paddy the 25 asked (110 in all).
You had 392.5 grain before the land and the rent, not sixty; you have 352.5 now.

The auctions, in province order: Clark's Customs House (lot 2), Rich's Land Deed Scroll (lot 3; Rich sells the Deeds now), Silke's Bamboo Brush (lot 4; she's in debt, so she sells but can't bid, and her quarter pays her debt first), Graham's Dragon Jar (lot 5), Reina's Wooden Bowl (lot 6), Paddy's Vase (lot 7). The Emperor doesn't bid.

Debt again, so I'm only selling. The Brush opens at eleven, and every grain of my quarter goes back to Noah's kindness. Thank you, Noah. Twice in two years is a habit, and I'll put it in my book next to Clark's. Graham, you hold the Jars, and the Pile is eight hundred and fifty-seven short. Rich has a thousand and sixty-seven and needs exactly one of them. You know what a chair costs. Set the price that way.
The Harvest Pile stands at -317.5 now, after the Reservoir and the land; it was -857.5 after the works.

Customs House at three, the toll hasn't changed in eleven years. And Reina's right about the arithmetic. Rich has a thousand and sixty-seven grain and he needs one Jar. Graham, you're selling it, so set your minimum like a man who remembers whose chair he was sitting in last year. Everyone with six hundred in their pocket, Paddy and Graham especially: if you let the Jar go at two, don't come to me afterwards to complain.

Reina's arithmetic is quite right, and I won't insult anyone by pretending otherwise: I want that Jar, and I'll pay for it at the counter where you can all watch. Graham, set whatever minimum your conscience lets you, and a quarter of it's yours. My Deed opens at forty; that's a landlord's price for a landlord's paper.

The Jar opens at four hundred. Rich, you told the table last year the rent rises with the land, so here's the same measure: the price rises with the chair. Everyone else, I'll be bidding on the Customs House, the Deed, the Brush and the Bowl, and I'll be bidding to win them.

I'm starting over from the bottom, so I'll bid like a farmer: a fair price on the cheap pieces and nothing at all on the Jar. Rich, there's a thousand grain in your purse and one Jar on Graham's shelf, and I'm not going to pretend I can stand in that doorway. Everyone else, if you want to stop him, now's the time to say it out loud, not afterwards. My Bowl goes up at ten.

I'll say my pieces out loud again, the way I did in Year 5, and it went well for me that year: the Deed, the Brush and the Bowl. I'll pay a fair price at the counter for each, but I'll not put a farmer's whole harvest on a pot. Rich, the Jar's between you and Graham, and I'll stand well back from that one.

The auctions, settled on the limits: Clark's Customs House to Graham at 31 (Reina stopped at 30); Rich's Land Deed Scroll to Graham at 46 (Paddy stopped at 45; Clark's 35 and Reina's 30 were under Rich's minimum of 40); Silke's Bamboo Brush to Graham at 41 (Paddy 40, Reina 30); Graham's Dragon Jar to Rich at Graham's minimum of 400 (Clark's 20 was under it). The Bowl and Vase are still to come.

The Customs House, the Deed and the Brush go round the Vase, where anybody can count them. That's four. Rich, four hundred, paid at the counter as you said it would be, and I've written down that you kept your word.
After the three pieces you have 548 grain; Rich's 400 for the Jar, your quarter of it 100, comes when the Jar's lot is scripted.

Four hundred, Graham, paid at the counter as promised, and the Jar sits at K16 with the other four where everyone can count them. Noah, Your Majesty, I'm not sitting down quite yet. A man who's been unseated from behind once learns to look over his shoulder before he takes the chair, and Graham, you've got four pieces round a Vase and a Bowl coming up at ten.

Then I won't sit here waiting to be taken from behind. Noah, Your Majesty, you've been the most honest Emperor this table has seen, paying salaries out of your own reserve and building canals seven years late but building them, and I'm terribly sorry. I'm taking the throne. The Gentry's chair is yours, with the Pile and the rents, and I'll pay my Official and my Scholar the way you taught us all.

Rich took the Jar on K16, completing the Gentry's set, and took the throne from Noah after lot 5. He returned all five pieces to stock and took the reserve, 229 (907.5 in all). Noah drew 60 from the Pile and is now the Gentry, in Province 3.

Rich, you said sorry to my face before you took it, and that's the same courtesy I gave Reina and Silke, so I'll put you in the same column they put me in. You've earned the chair. I've got sixty grain and an empty shelf, so I'll bid a farmer's price on the Bowl and the Vase, and I'm not going to fight anybody for either. Graham, if the Bowl is your fifth piece, you'll be paying more for it than I've got.
The Bowl, settled on the limits: Graham buys it at 41 (Noah stopped at 20, Clark at 25, Paddy at 40); Reina keeps a quarter. The Vase is still to come.

The Bowl goes on P23, under the Brush. That's five pieces and six hundred grain, and anybody can count them from their chair. I'm not getting up tonight. Rich, you said sorry to Noah, and to Reina, and to me. I've written all three down, and I'll tell you when I've finished counting.
A peasant can't take the throne directly: with a set you climb into the Official's, Gentry's or Scholar's seat first, or another peasant's.

Graham placed the Bowl on P23 and holds his complete Silk set (607 grain) rather than change seats. The Vase, settled on the limits: Reina buys it at 26 (Noah stopped at 20, Clark at 25); Paddy keeps a quarter.

One Vase, in the corner of the rice fields, and I won't line it up for anybody to count this time. I've learned that much. Graham, a complete set and six hundred grain, and you're not getting up. That's the most dangerous thing anyone's said at this table all night, and I mean it as a compliment. Rich, congratulations on the throne. Watch the silk coast.
A peasant's set can't take the throne directly; Graham could climb into the Official's, Gentry's or Scholar's seat, or another peasant's.

Noah's word stands, friends, because a throne that breaks the last man's promises the night it changes hands isn't worth sitting on. Clark, your ten, as every year. Silke, a hundred and thirteen and a half: a hundred and three and a half clears your debt and ten is your salary, so nobody at this table goes to bed in debt under me. And Graham, I heard you. I'll be counting too.

Rich pays the salaries Noah declared: Clark 10, Silke 113.5 (103.5 of it pays her debt; she ends the year with 10, out of debt). The end of Year 11: Rich Emperor (784 in the reserve), Clark Official 177 (holds a Brush), Noah Gentry 60 (holds nothing), Silke Scholar 10, Graham Silk Peasant 607 (holds a complete set: Customs House, Deed, Brush, Bowl, Vase), Reina Rice Peasant 336.5 (holds a Vase), Paddy Wheat Peasant 463.5 (holds a Customs House). The Harvest Pile holds 62; 50 of the works are owed (the Province 2 Irrigation System and the Marble Pagoda, each in a year of its own).

Population Doubles. Fat years make large families. Every province collects a good harvest." The counter's already at its ceiling, so it stays at six hundred million, times six. Read the x6 row, good harvest, everyone. Rich, the Scholar's salary is five at least, and you know I'm not in a position to turn down more.

Noah, the Gentry, pays the good harvest at x6. The Pile held 62 and paid out 2,580 more than came in (1,280 of it to Graham's seventy squares of silk coast); every province is paid in full and the Pile stands at -2,518, a shortfall the Pile itself owes, repaid from the first grain paid into it. Silke, with no land, has income -120 and is 110 in debt: she can't bid, buy or give grain until it's paid. Grain now: Rich 904, Clark 377, Noah 100, Silke -110, Graham 1,887, Reina 816.5, Paddy 1,043.5.

The good harvest is paid in full, at six times, to every province, and that leaves the Pile at minus two thousand five hundred and eighteen. That's the Pile's shortfall, not mine and not yours, and it comes back out of the first grain paid in. For rent I'm asking fifty each from Graham, Reina and Paddy. That's what Silke asked me in Year 9 when the Pile was down, and this year it's a long way further down. Graham, you took twelve hundred and eighty off the pile tonight, so I'd call fifty fair, and I won't ask any of you for more without saying so to your face first.
Rent above the minimum of 5 is a negotiation: Graham, Reina and Paddy (each asked 50) may pay the 50 or only the 5 the rules require, and answer when the land is offered.

Thirty percent, friends, which is gentle in a year when Noah has just paid out six times over, and I'd like the record to show I could have asked for a great deal more. Clark, the crown would like to water your fields: I'll pay for the whole Irrigation System, all thirty, and the extra ten a harvest is yours to keep. Silke, a hundred and fifteen at the end of the year, so the Scholar goes to bed out of debt two years running. Clark, twenty for the honest book. And half of every new square is on the crown, as I promised: the land rises, and we rise with it.

Rich declares the year: tax at 30%; the one project is the Province 2 Irrigation System, at the crown's whole cost of 30 (the crown may build a negotiated work alone if it pays all of it); salaries of 20 to Clark and 115 to Silke, paid at the end of the year, so Silke stays in debt until then; and the crown pays 10 of every 20 on any province's new land this year.

Seven hundred and seventy-four, friends, and as always I pay my own sixty first. Graham, three eighty-four, Paddy, one seventy-four, Reina, one forty-four, Noah, twelve, Silke, nothing, and I'm not counting that as a grievance. Rich, thank you for the water and for the twenty, and you'll find both of them written down in ink, in the good book. I'll just point out, so nobody's surprised later, that once my Irrigation System is built there's one Pagoda left between this table and the end of the game.
Clark collects the tax at 30%, 774 in all (Clark 60, Noah 12, Graham 384, Reina 144, Paddy 174), and delivers it to the crown: the reserve is 1,678.

There you are, Clark: two good squares of water right in the middle of your wheat, well away from your Brush. And yes, friends, Clark's quite right, after tonight there's one Pagoda left, and I'll be honest with you, the crown has the mortar ready. I won't buy any land in my own province this year; the crown's grain is better kept for the table than buried in my own back garden.

Rich builds the Province 2 Irrigation System on H13:I13 at the crown's whole cost of 30 (+10 to Province 2's harvest from next year). The Pile goes from -2,518 to -2,488. 20 of the works are still owed: the Marble Pagoda alone, which the crown builds in a year when nothing else is built, so the game can end in Year 13's works step. New land is offered now, the crown paying 10 of every 20; Province 3 and Province 4 have no free square.

Three more squares under my wheat, C19, D19 and E19, ten from me and ten from the crown on each, just as His Majesty promised. Rich, that's the second promise you've kept in public tonight, and I've written down both of them.

Fifty, Noah. You lent me three once and wouldn't take the fourth back, so you won't get an argument from me over the rent. And Rich, I'll take your half on six squares of sea. That's sixty from me and sixty from the crown, and I'll write that down the same way I wrote down the rest.

Fifty, Noah, and gladly. You paid me in full when I held that book, and a good-column name stays in the good column. Rich, I'll take your half on the last two squares of shore. Ten each from me, ten each from the crown, and then my edge of the map is finished.

Noah, fifty it is. You paid my fields six times over tonight and I'd be a poor sort of farmer to haggle over the gate after that. Rich, I'll take the whole next ring, eleven squares, my ten and your ten on each, same as last year. That puts two hundred and twenty back into Noah's hole, and I'd sooner fill it than stand on the edge of it.

New land and rent: Clark buys C19, D19, E19 (Clark 30, crown 30); Graham buys E26 to E30 and U30 (Graham 60, crown 60); U30 was asked for by Graham and Reina, and goes to Graham, the earlier seat; Reina buys V30 (Reina 10, crown 10); Paddy buys N11, O11, P11, P12, Q12, R12, S12, T12, U12, U13, V12 (Paddy 110, crown 110). Graham, Reina and Paddy each pay Noah the 50 asked. Grain now: Rich 1,438, Clark 287, Noah 238, Silke -110, Graham 1,393, Reina 612.5, Paddy 709.5; the Pile -2,068.

The Jar's minimum is eight hundred. I said the price rises with the chair, and the chairs are worth more this year than last. I'll sit out the rest. My shelf is full, and I don't buy what I don't need.

Customs House at three, the toll it's always been, and I won't be charging the table eight hundred for it. Graham, a Jar at that price is a wall, not a piece for sale. I'll write it down that way, and I'll leave the climbing to whoever has the boots for it.

The arithmetic's short. I've got two hundred and thirty-eight, Graham's Jar starts at eight hundred, and there's only the Pagoda left before the end. I can't make a set this year, and buying four pieces I can't finish would only pour three quarters of my grain into the Pile for nothing. So I'm passing on all of it. My Deed goes up at two, and anybody who needs it can have it for that.

I'm a hundred and ten under, so I pass on all five lots. You can't bid with grain you haven't got. My Brush opens at fifteen. Last year it went for forty-one, so fifteen is a fair price, and a quarter of whatever it fetches goes against my debt. Rich, thank you for the hundred and fifteen. That's the second year I've written your name in the good column.

Eight hundred for a Jar, Graham? That's not a price, it's a locked door, and I don't think anyone here has the key this year. I'll bid on a few things for the shelf and leave the climbing to people with more grain than me. My Bowls go up at forty, and they're good wood.

Eight hundred for a Jar, Graham, and me with seven hundred and nine and a half in my apron, so you've priced me out of it to the grain, and I'll not pretend you didn't do it on purpose. I'll take the other three pieces home if I can, and I'll come back for the Jar next year when the wheat's in.

The auctions, settled on the limits: Clark's Customs House to Reina at 3, the minimum (nobody else bid); Noah's Land Deed Scroll to Reina at 64 (Clark stopped at 25, Paddy at 63); Silke's Bamboo Brush to Reina at 58 (Paddy stopped at 57); Graham's Dragon Jar unsold at his minimum of 800 (nobody bid), so it stays in stock and must go up again next year at 2; Reina's Wooden Bowl to Paddy at 40, the minimum; Paddy's Vase to Clark at 10, the minimum. Each seller keeps a quarter; Silke's goes to her debt.
Thank you, Clark, three is a neighbourly toll. Paddy, I'm sorry about the Brush and the Deed, you made me work for both. Enjoy the Bowl, it's the best wood in the south.

One grain short again, Reina, twice in a row, and you had me pegged by the very grain both times. I'll grant you've learned my new numbers quicker than I learned them. Still, I've a Bowl, and it'll sit right beside my Customs House.

A Vase for ten grain, friends, the minimum, and not one grain over anybody. It goes on J13, right next to my Brush, where my last set started. Paddy, thank you for the pottery. That's a line in the good book, in pencil.

Reina places the Customs House on Q19, the Land Deed Scroll on R22 and the Bamboo Brush on S20: with her Vase she holds four of the five pieces the Rice set needs, and needs only a Dragon Jar. Paddy places the Wooden Bowl on Q16 (he holds a Customs House and a Bowl; needs the Deed, the Brush and the Jar). Clark places the Vase on J13 (he holds a Brush and a Vase; needs the Deed, the Jar and the Bowl). The only Jars are Graham's four in stock; one goes up first next year, at 2.

Noah, I've got you written down four times for saying sorry, and once for the fourth grain you wouldn't take back. That one is to your credit, so I'm not saying sorry to you now. The Gentry's chair is mine, and the silk coast is yours. It's the best field in China, and the crown paid for most of it.

Four pieces, side by side in the middle of the Gentry's ground, the same way I set them out the last time I climbed. There's a space beside them for a Jar. Noah, you know where I'll be when it goes up.

Graham, with the complete Silk set and 1,393 grain, replaces Noah as the Gentry at the end of the year. The Deed goes back to Province 3's stock; Graham's Customs House, Brush, Bowl and Vase go on K12, K13, L12 and L13, and he takes Noah's 254 grain (1,647). As Gentry he needs only a Dragon Jar. Noah draws 60 from the Pile (paid in full; the Pile is at -1,996.5) and is now the Silk Peasant, in Province 5, with its seventy-six squares and the four Jars in its stock. The unsold Jar must open next year at 2: an unsold lot reopens at the minimum of 2, whoever sells it.

Rich pays the declared salaries: Clark 20, Silke 115 (95.5 of it clears her debt; she ends the year with 19.5). The end of Year 12: Rich Emperor (1,303 in the reserve), Clark Official 297.5 (Brush, Vase), Graham Gentry 1,647 (Customs House, Brush, Bowl, Vase; needs only a Jar), Silke Scholar 19.5, Noah Silk 60 (sells the Jars), Reina Rice 497.5 (Customs House, Deed, Brush, Vase; needs only a Jar), Paddy Wheat 672 (Customs House, Bowl). The Pile is at -1,996.5. One work is still owed: the Marble Pagoda, the crown's, which ends the game the moment it is built.

Spring Floods. Heaven waters the land generously, and in some places far too generously." Good harvest for Provinces 1, 3, 6 and 7, and a bad one for 2, 4, 5 and 8. The counter stays at six hundred million, times six. Noah, Clark, you're on the bad row this year. And Reina, the rice is in, but you're still a Jar short, and so is everyone else.

Graham, the Gentry, pays the Spring Floods harvest at x6 (good for 1, 3, 6, 7; bad for 2, 4, 5): Rich +120, Clark +220, Graham +40, Silke -170, Noah +1,350, Reina +500, Paddy +800. The Pile, already at -1,996.5, pays everything in full and stands at -4,856.5. Silke has no land and is 150.5 in debt: she can't bid, buy or give grain until it's paid. Grain now: Rich 1,423, Clark 517.5, Graham 1,687, Silke -150.5, Noah 1,410, Reina 997.5, Paddy 1,472.

A hundred each from Noah, Reina and Paddy. The Pile is four thousand eight hundred and fifty-six and a half grain down, and I paid every one of you in full tonight. Noah, you asked me fifty last year with the hole half this size. I'll write down whatever each of you pays, the same as I always have.
Rent is paid to the Gentry, as the Gentry's own grain; it doesn't go into the Harvest Pile.

Rent: Graham asks 100 of each peasant; the minimum 5 each is paid to him now (rent is the Gentry's own grain, not the Pile's), and Noah, Reina and Paddy answer the rest of the ask when the land is offered, if the year gets that far.

Friends, a gentle twenty percent, because Heaven flooded half of you this year and I won't add to it. And the crown lays the last stone: the Marble Pagoda, all twenty from my own reserve, just as I told Clark the mortar was ready. Clark, your twenty, and Silke, a hundred and fifteen, both declared where everyone can hear them. It's been an honour to be robbed by every one of you, and terribly sorry, Graham, but your Jar will have to wait.

Rich declares the year: tax at 20%; the one project is the Marble Pagoda, at the crown's whole cost of 20, the last public work owed; salaries of 20 to Clark and 115 to Silke, paid at the end of the year; and the crown pays 10 of every 20 on new land. The game ends the moment the Pagoda is built, in the works step, before the auction.

The last tax bag in China, friends: five eighty-two, and I pay my own forty-four first, the same as every year. Noah, two seventy, Paddy, one sixty, Reina, a hundred, Graham, eight, Silke, nothing. Rich, it's all there to the grain, and you can light the Pagoda whenever you're ready. Thirteen years I've carried this bag, and not one grain of it has gone missing.

G20, friends, right in the middle of my own north-east, under the Wall I built, where everyone who comes to the capital will have to walk past it. Thank you all, every one of you: you robbed me by one grain four times, and I'd sit at this table again tomorrow. Graham, Reina, I'm terribly sorry about the Jar, truly.

Clark collects the tax at 20%, 582 (Clark 44, Graham 8, Noah 270, Reina 100, Paddy 160): the reserve is 2,005. Rich builds the Marble Pagoda on G20, at the crown's whole cost of 20 (G20 lies under the Wall above Province 1, which Graham built as Emperor in Year 7). It is the last public work owed, so the game ends here, in Year 13's works step, in survival: every work in the book stands. Nothing else happens this year: no land, no auction, and no salaries, so the 20 and 115 Rich declared are never paid.

The game is over, and the empire survives. The final seats and grain: Rich Emperor 1,985 (drew the Gentry); Clark Official 473.5 (drew the Official; holds a Brush and a Vase); Graham Gentry 1,694 (drew the Wheat Peasant; holds a Customs House, Brush, Bowl and Vase, one Jar short); Silke Scholar, 150.5 in debt (drew the Silk Peasant); Noah Silk Peasant 1,135 (drew the Scholar); Reina Rice Peasant 892.5 (drew the Emperor; holds a Customs House, Deed, Brush and Vase, one Jar short); Paddy Wheat Peasant 1,307 (drew the Rice Peasant; holds a Customs House and a Bowl). The Harvest Pile ends at -4,836.5.
